studies.title: The Command Has Already Come
studies.meaning: The surah opens with a completed past tense for something still ahead: God's command has come. Commentators read this as certainty stated as fact, answering listeners who kept demanding that the promised reckoning arrive on their schedule. The instruction not to hurry it follows immediately. Then the subject turns to what God does send down now, angels carrying the Spirit to servants of His choosing, with a single commission attached: warn that there is no god but Him.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the later years in the city when opposition had hardened into mockery. The classical sources describe opponents challenging the Prophet to produce the punishment he warned of, treating its delay as proof that nothing was coming. The surah opens by answering that taunt directly, then spends its whole first stretch on evidence already in front of them rather than on the reckoning they had demanded.

keyTerms.note: The word covers both an order given and the matter it concerns, so the phrase can mean the decree God has issued and the event that decree brings about. Commentators keep both senses.
Read here as revelation itself, life-giving to hearts as breath is to bodies, or as the angel who carries it. The two readings sit together in the classical commentaries without conflict.
A form that means asking for something to be brought forward, not merely feeling impatient. It names a demand made out loud, which is what the opponents were doing when they called for the reckoning.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a society where few could read, a warning travelled by voice, and the word for warner named a real role. A man who spotted a raiding party from a ridge would run ahead of it into the settlement shouting, stripped of his cloak so that no one could mistake him for a traveller. Warning was urgent, unpaid and often unwelcome. The commission given in these ayat borrows exactly that role.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb that opens this surah is a perfect, the form Arabic uses for completed action, although the event it announces had not yet occurred. Classical grammarians treat this as a way of stating a future certainty as though it were already finished. Surah 21 opens with the same move, announcing that the reckoning of humankind has drawn near.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are held together here. God's decree is fixed and its timing is not the listener's to set, which removes the argument that delay means absence. And revelation is described as something sent down by choice, on servants God selects, rather than earned or achieved. Prophecy is therefore not a rank a person climbs to. The content of every such sending is compressed into one sentence, so the message stays constant wherever the messengers differ.

crossReferences.why: Opens another surah with the same perfect-tense announcement of something that has not yet arrived.
Places the same construction at the head of a surah, saying the reckoning of humankind has drawn near.
Calls revelation a spirit sent by God's command to one who did not know the Book before.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you treat a delay as a cancellation. A reply that has not come, a result still pending, a change you were promised. Give it a name and set it down for a day without deciding what the silence means. The passage is not asking you for patience in general. It is asking you to stop reading absence into waiting.

studies.title: From A Drop To Adversary
studies.meaning: Three acts of creation in three sentences, descending in scale. The heavens and the earth are made with truth, meaning purposefully rather than as a game. Then the human being, traced back to a residue of fluid, who turns out to be an open disputant. Commentators dwell on the jolt between the humblest possible origin and the confidence with which such a creature argues against its Maker. Then livestock, where the emphasis shifts from origin to use: warmth, benefits, food.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, part of the surah's opening catalogue of things its audience could check by looking. The argument being answered is not denial of God; the Meccans acknowledged a creator and attached partners to Him. So the passage does not set out to prove that God exists. It lists what He alone made, then names the human response as dispute, which is what the surah's first hearers were audibly doing.

keyTerms.note: The word names the small quantity of water left in a vessel or a skin, the residue rather than the pour. Choosing it sets the origin of a practised arguer at the smallest imaginable scale.

An intensive form. Not someone who happens to disagree but someone skilled at contention. Paired with a word meaning plain or open, it describes argument conducted in daylight rather than resentment held quietly.
A collective covering camels, cattle, sheep and goats together, the animals a household lived from. Its root carries softness and ease, and gives Arabic its ordinary word for a blessing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A household's wealth was counted in animals, and one herd supplied nearly everything. Hair and wool became tents and cloaks, hides became water skins and sandals, milk and meat were the food, and dung was fuel where there was no wood. The word this passage uses for warmth points first at clothing. Losing a herd to drought or to a raid did not reduce a family's comfort; it ended it.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase translated as an open adversary occurs in only two places in the Quran, here and at 36:77, and both times it follows the same sentence about a human being made from a drop of fluid. The wording is nearly identical in the two surahs, which the commentators note as a deliberate echo rather than a repetition.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Creation is said to be with truth, a phrase the commentators gloss as purpose and justice rather than accuracy. That rules out a universe made for amusement and makes a reckoning coherent. The human being is then placed inside that ordered world at a strange angle: the one creature whose origin is smallest and whose objections are loudest. Nothing is said about whether the dispute is fair. It is simply recorded as the characteristic human move.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the drop-to-adversary sentence and answers the argument it goes on to make about bones.
States directly that the heavens and the earth were not created in play, which is what creation with truth denies.
Returns to the same origin, a mingled drop, and reads it as the beginning of a test rather than an insult.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you argued about this week where you were sure you were right. Do not revisit whether you were. Instead spend a minute on the plain fact that the person holding that certainty began as almost nothing and will not be here in a century. The passage puts those two facts side by side without resolving them. Sit where it puts you.

studies.title: Beauty At Dusk And Dawn
studies.meaning: After the useful comes the beautiful. The same animals that gave warmth and food are now said to give beauty, and the beauty is fixed to two particular hours: when the herd comes home in the evening and when it goes out in the morning. Commentators point out that no practical benefit is attached to this one. Then usefulness returns, in loads carried to places a person on foot would reach only at severe cost.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, inside the run of ayat listing what the audience already possessed, before the surah turns to argument. Mecca sat in a valley without crops, dependent on caravans for grain and on herds for nearly everything else. These two ayat name the two things such a life ran on: the sight of the animals coming back at evening, and their ability to cross ground people could not cross alone.

keyTerms.note: Not ornament but a beauty of proportion and fullness, used of a well-formed animal and of a scene in good order. The ayah lists it as a benefit in its own right, beside food and clothing.
From the root for rest and for evening. It names the hour when herds return to the fold, the one moment of the day when the whole flock is visible at once and a household counts what came back.
From a root meaning to split. The phrase pictures effort that divides a person, a cost paid out of the self rather than out of a purse, which is what a long march without an animal was.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Herding ran on two moments. At first light the animals were driven out to pasture, and at dusk they were brought back and penned, which was when losses showed. A camel could carry across a desert stage a load that would have killed the man carrying it himself, and the routes north to Syria and south to Yemen existed only because of that. Beauty and freight were the same animal.
studies.didYouKnow: The two verbs in this ayah, one for driving a herd out in the morning and one for bringing it home at evening, each occur exactly once in the whole Quran, and both occurrences are in this single sentence. The Quran has other words for morning and evening; these two belong specifically to the movement of animals.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A list of benefits pauses to name something that serves no purpose. Beauty is presented as part of the provision rather than a by-product of it, which says the arrangement of the world is not merely functional. The passage then closes with two divine names, one meaning tender kindness and the other mercy, attached to a description of freight and distance. Care of that quality is being claimed at the level of ordinary logistics.

crossReferences.why: Runs the same catalogue of livestock benefits and closes by asking why gratitude does not follow.
Names riding, eating, and reaching a need in the breast as purposes served by the herds.
Draws the same line from milk and meat to being carried, on animals and then on ships.

studies.applyIt: Find the hour in your day that corresponds to the herd coming home. The moment things stop moving and you can see what is there. Do not use it to plan or to review. Look at one ordinary thing in front of you and let it be pleasant rather than useful. That is the whole content of the middle of this passage.

studies.title: And He Creates What You Do Not Know
studies.meaning: Three more animals are listed, and this time riding and display are both named as purposes without embarrassment. The sentence then opens outwards: God creates things you have no knowledge of, which the commentators take as a standing clause covering whatever is not yet known. The second ayah turns from roads to the road. God undertakes to make the direct way plain, some ways deviate from it, and had He willed, everyone would have been guided.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is still working through what its audience could verify, and horses, mules and donkeys were nearer to Meccan life than to the desert interior, being animals of settled trade rather than long crossings. The turn in the second ayah is the surah's first move from evidence to response, and it arrives without transition, which is characteristic of this chapter's method throughout.

keyTerms.note: The word for what is added to make a thing look well. Listing it beside transport, with no criticism attached, sets the passage apart from the places where adornment is treated as a distraction.
From a root meaning to aim straight and to keep to a middle. The phrase pictures a road that goes where it says it goes, as opposed to one that bends away without announcing it.
Used of a road that leaves the true line and of a ruler who departs from justice. The same word covers both, so a crooked path and a crooked judgement are described identically.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Horses were expensive and scarce in Mecca, kept for prestige and for raiding rather than for haulage, while mules and donkeys did the short work between town and well. A man's mount announced his standing before he spoke. Meanwhile the caravan routes were real roads with real branches, and taking the wrong fork out of a valley could add days to a journey or end it. Guidance was first a matter of tracks.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase this ayah uses for the direct road occurs only once in the Quran. Elsewhere the same idea is carried by the word for a straight path, which appears dozens of times. The commentators note that the unusual wording pairs a road with the human faculty of aiming, so the ayah is about direction taken as much as about the route itself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The closing clause is left deliberately unresolved. God could have guided everyone and did not, which the classical commentators handle without flattening either side: the capacity is affirmed and the choice not to exercise it is not explained away. Alongside it stands the statement that showing the direct way rests with God, so guidance is a gift rather than an achievement. Between those two lies room for both effort and dependence, which is where the tradition leaves it.

crossReferences.why: States the same possibility, that all on earth could have believed, and forbids compelling them into it.
Uses almost the same construction to say that guidance is upon God, and closes a different argument with it.
Contrasts one straight path with the many other paths that scatter a traveller away from it.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you own mainly because it looks well, and let yourself stop apologising for it. This passage lists display beside transport without a word of criticism. Then notice where the apology actually belongs in your week, which is usually somewhere else entirely. Naming the difference honestly is more useful than a general suspicion of everything pleasant.

studies.title: Water, And What Grows From It
studies.meaning: One substance is sent down and the passage follows it into two uses that do not look alike. First it is simply drink. Then it becomes the trees among which herds are pastured, and after that grain, olives, dates, grapes and every other kind of fruit. The list moves from what keeps a person alive today to what a farmer waits a season for. It closes by saying this is a sign, and specifies the audience: people who think.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Mecca had no agriculture of its own, so the crops in this list belonged to Ta'if and the oases the Meccans traded with rather than to the valley they lived in. The audience knew these fruits as goods arriving, which sharpens the point: the same water that fell somewhere else produced everything they bought, and no one in the chain of purchase had made any of it.

keyTerms.note: A plain word for anything drunk, placed first and left undeveloped. The ordering matters: the passage gives water its simplest use before it gives the elaborate ones, and does not rank them.
A verb meaning to send animals out to graze freely, from a root connected with marking. It names a whole system of feeding that costs the owner nothing except the decision to open the pen.

A form suggesting turning something over repeatedly rather than a single insight. The sign is described as available only to sustained attention, which is why the audience is specified rather than assumed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water arrived twice a year at best, in short violent falls that ran off the rock and filled the wadis for a few hours. Wells were owned, named and fought over, and the right to water a herd could be inherited or bought. Grain, olives and dates came into Mecca on camels from Syria, Yemen and Ta'if. Nobody in that valley could imagine water as a background condition. It was an event that people watched for.
studies.didYouKnow: The formula that closes this ayah, calling something a sign for a people who use a named faculty, appears six times in the Quran with the singular word for sign, and five of those six are in this surah. The other stands in surah 27. Surah 16 uses it as a refrain, changing only the faculty it addresses each time.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Rain is used here as the standing argument, and its force is that it cannot be claimed by anyone. Nothing in the chain from cloud to fruit is a human product, yet the result is described as being for you, which places dependence and generosity in the same sentence. Naming the sign for people who think also sets a condition. The evidence is public and the conclusion is not automatic; something is asked of the observer.

crossReferences.why: Asks directly who sends the water down from the cloud, and offers to make it bitter.
Runs a nearly identical list of crops and closes it as provision for people and their livestock.
Follows the same water into grain, dates and olives, and asks the reader to look at the fruit ripening.

studies.applyIt: The next glass of water you drink, drink the first mouthful without doing anything else. Not as a ritual, just as an experiment in noticing. The passage puts drink first in its list and spends no words defending the choice. Most people find the ordinary things are the ones they have never once attended to, and water is the most ordinary of them.

studies.title: The Sun, The Moon, The Stars
studies.meaning: The list rises from the ground to the sky. Night and day, sun and moon are put at the service of human beings, and then the stars are described in a slightly different grammar: they are harnessed by God's command, which the commentators read as underlining that nothing in the arrangement is self-directed. The second ayah drops back to earth for the sheer variety of colours in what was scattered across it. Each closes with a different faculty named.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The audience lived by these bodies rather than looking at them: prayer times, market days, caravan departures and the pilgrimage season were all read off the sun and the moon, and night navigation across open country was done by stars. Nothing in the ayat asks for new information. They ask that things already used daily be counted as evidence, which is the method of the whole opening section.

keyTerms.note: Used of setting an animal or a worker to a task without payment. Applied to the sun and the moon it says they are working, on a schedule not their own, for a benefit that is not theirs.
A verb for creating by spreading widely, used of seed broadcast by hand. It implies profusion rather than assembly, which suits a sentence whose whole subject is variety.
From the root for remembrance. It suggests recovering something already known rather than learning something new, so the faculty addressed by the colours of the earth is recollection.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caravan leaving Mecca for Syria travelled at night in summer to spare the animals, and the route was held by stars rather than by landmarks, which vanish in the dark. Guides who could hold a bearing across sand at night were paid well and remembered by name. The moon set the months and therefore the sacred seasons in which fighting stopped. Both bodies were instruments before they were ornaments.
studies.didYouKnow: The formula closing the second of these ayat, a sign for a people who take heed, occurs only twice in the Quran, here and in surah 6. Each ayah in this stretch of surah 16 closes with a different mental verb, moving through thinking, reasoning and remembering, so the same evidence is offered three times to three different faculties.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing the heavenly bodies under a verb used of hired labour empties them of divinity in one word, which mattered in a setting where the sun and the moon were worshipped elsewhere in the region. What is left is a working system, ordered and useful, whose usefulness is the argument. The variety of colours then adds something the order alone would not: the arrangement is not only efficient. It is more elaborate than function requires.

crossReferences.why: Forbids bowing to the sun and moon while pointing at the One who created them, on the same logic.
Uses the identical verb for the sun, moon and stars being harnessed by God's command.
Develops the theme of differing colours through mountains, people and animals, and links it to knowledge.

studies.applyIt: Go outside tonight and find one thing overhead you can name. The moon's phase will do. Then work out what it was doing for someone a thousand years ago in your position, with no clock and no calendar. The passage rests on things that were once instruments and have become scenery. Recovering one of them as an instrument takes about a minute.

studies.title: The Sea Made To Serve
studies.meaning: One ayah takes the sea through four uses and ends by naming the response it expects. Fresh meat comes out of it, and ornaments people put on, and ships are seen cutting through it while human beings go looking for God's bounty. The last clause is the point of the sentence: so that you may give thanks. Everything before it is evidence. The commentators note that seeking bounty is described as human work done inside a provision no one arranged.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and worth noticing that Mecca is inland. The Red Sea coast was two days away at Jeddah and Shu'ayba, and Meccan trade reached the sea through those ports and along it toward Abyssinia. Pearls came up the same routes. The audience knew the sea as the edge of their commercial world rather than as daily scenery, which is why the ayah lists what comes from it rather than describing it.

keyTerms.note: A word for meat still soft and newly taken, used of fish. In a climate where meat had to be dried or eaten at once, freshness was the specific luxury, and the ayah names it rather than assuming it.
Covers pearls and coral brought up by divers. Adornment is listed as a benefit alongside food, without qualification, which the commentators read as an ordinary permission rather than an argument.
A form describing ships pushing water aside so that it parts audibly at the bow. The word carries the sound as much as the motion, which is why translators reach for ploughing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Pearl diving in the Red Sea and the Gulf was old work, done on a held breath with a stone for descent and a rope for return, and the best beds were known and defended. Dried fish travelled inland, but fresh fish did not, so a Meccan tasted it only near the coast. Grain from Egypt and cloth from further off came by ship to Jeddah and then by camel up to the valley.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for ships cleaving the water appears in only two places in the Quran, here and in surah 35, and both passages pair it with the ornaments taken from the sea and with the search for God's bounty. Surah 35 adds the detail that two seas, one sweet and one salt, both yield the same things.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The closing clause makes thankfulness the intended outcome of the whole list, which frames gratitude as a form of accurate perception rather than a mood. Seeking bounty is placed inside the same sentence as being given it, so human effort is not set against divine provision but located within it. The sea is a useful case for this, being the one environment where no amount of labour changes what is actually there to be found.

crossReferences.why: Runs the same list of fresh meat, ornaments and cleaving ships, and extends it to two different seas.
States the principle the closing clause depends on, that gratitude is answered with increase.
Describes God driving ships at sea so that people may seek His bounty, in nearly the same words.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you ate today and trace it backwards as far as you honestly can: the shop, the lorry, the field or the boat, the weather that season. Stop when you run out of knowledge rather than at a tidy conclusion. The ayah does the same work in one sentence, and the point of it is the last clause, which arrives only after the tracing is done.

studies.title: Is The Maker Like The Made
studies.meaning: Mountains are set into the earth so that it does not sway with its inhabitants, and rivers and roads are added so that people find their way. Then landmarks, and the star by which travellers hold a bearing. Having built the whole apparatus of orientation, the passage asks one question and stops: is the one who creates like the one who creates nothing. No answer is supplied. The commentators treat the silence after it as the argument.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the surah's long opening catalogue. The question at the end is aimed at a specific practice rather than at unbelief in general: the Meccans acknowledged a creator and also served objects that had been carved, and the ayah puts those two facts next to each other. It is the hinge of the chapter, and everything after it argues from the position this question establishes.

keyTerms.note: From a root used of a ship riding steady at anchor. The word describes weight that holds something else still, so mountains are named by their function rather than by their height.
The verb for the unsteady motion of a ship or of a person about to lose their footing. It belongs to the same picture as the anchoring word beside it, and the two are usually paired.
Landmarks used for navigation, a rock or a ridge that tells a traveller where they are. The word shares a root with knowledge, so a landmark is literally a thing that informs.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Desert travel was navigation, not walking. A guide read dunes, rock formations and the colour of gravel by day, and at night held a course by particular stars near the pole. Losing the line by a few degrees over a long stage meant missing a well, which was fatal. Families paid for guides the way they paid for water. The ayat name exactly the tools of that trade and then ask who supplied them.
studies.didYouKnow: The preceding ayah in this surah used the plural for stars, describing them as harnessed by God's command; this one switches to the singular. The singular form appears in four places in the Quran, and this is the only one where it means the star a traveller steers by. The classical commentators note the shift and read it as pointing to whichever star holds a bearing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The closing question defines God by an activity rather than by a quality. What separates the Creator from everything else is not power in the abstract but the fact of having originated something, and the objects being contrasted are ones the audience had made themselves. Placing the question after a list of navigational aids is deliberate: the passage has just shown that finding your way depends on things you did not put there, and then asks what you turn to.

crossReferences.why: Presses the same contrast further, saying the invoked objects could not create even a fly.
Has Abraham ask whether people worship what they carve, when God created them and their handiwork.
Uses the same image of the earth spread out and mountains set as pegs holding it steady.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you rely on that you had no part in making, and one thing you rely on that you built yourself. Hold them next to each other for a moment without ranking them. This passage does not ask you to despise what people make. It asks you to keep straight which of the two you are leaning on when the ground moves.

studies.title: The Dead Things People Call On
studies.meaning: The four ayat move by steps. Favours are declared past counting and the sentence closes, unexpectedly, on forgiveness and mercy, which the commentators read as covering the shortfall in thanks that must follow. Then knowledge of what is hidden and what is shown. Then the objects people invoke are stripped of everything: they create nothing, they are themselves created, they are dead rather than alive, and they do not even know when they will be raised.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a surah that spends its opening third listing what God has made and given: rain, cattle, the sea, mountains, stars for navigation. This passage is the turn from the list to its conclusion. The audience in Mecca maintained shrines and images that were tended, dressed and consulted, and the argument here works by taking them seriously enough to ask what they can actually do. No specific occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A singular noun given to a whole people to count, so the grammar sets one blessing against many counters and still says the tally fails. The root also gives the words for softness and ease.
From the root for a secret and for the innermost part of a thing. Placed against its opposite in the same clause, it covers the whole range from an unspoken thought to a public declaration.

The plural is the ordinary word for the dead, applied here to carved objects that were never alive. Using a word that implies a former life sharpens the contrast with the living God named throughout the surah.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sanctuary at Mecca held images that had names, histories and custodial families. People brought them offerings before a journey and consulted them by drawing marked arrows before a marriage or a raid. Caring for one was a paid office and a source of standing. To call these objects dead in front of the men who fed and clothed them was not an abstract argument; it named a household trade.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah is named for a creature that appears in only two of its ayat, in a passage on the bee that is inspired to build in hills and trees. It is sometimes called the surah of blessings because of how much of it lists what has been given. This passage sits at the hinge where the listing turns into an argument.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument is made on the ground of capability rather than of authority. Nothing is said about what the objects deserve; the question asked is what they can do, and the answer works backwards from creation to existence to life to knowledge. Set against that, the opening clause about uncounted favours becomes evidence rather than sentiment: the case for God rests on what has been given, and the case against the idols on what has not.

crossReferences.why: The other place the uncountable-blessings sentence appears, closing on the human verdict instead.
Presses the same test further: they could not create a fly, or take one back.
Says the invoked ones do not hear, and would disown the association on the Day.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you already own and trace it backwards. Your cup: clay or sand, a kiln, a driver, a shop, someone who chose it. Follow the chain until you get bored. Then notice that you did this for one object out of the several hundred in your house. That is the shape of the claim this passage makes about counting.

studies.title: Hearts In Denial
studies.meaning: A short statement of oneness is followed by a diagnosis. Those who do not believe in the hereafter are described by two things at once: their hearts refuse, and they are swollen with self-importance. Commentators read the order as causal in either direction, since refusal breeds pride and pride produces refusal. What is striking is that unbelief is located in the heart rather than in the reasoning, and named as a posture rather than a conclusion.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, immediately after the surah has dismissed the objects people invoked as things that create nothing and are themselves dead. This ayah supplies the positive statement those denials were clearing space for. The classical commentators connect the arrogance named here to the specific social position of the Meccan leadership, who stood to lose standing if the message were accepted, rather than to arrogance as a general failing.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to find something unfamiliar and reject it. It describes a heart that does not merely disbelieve a claim but treats it as foreign, which is a reaction rather than a judgement.
A form meaning to seek greatness for oneself, to act big. The grammar implies claiming a size you do not have, so the fault is inflation rather than actual eminence.
The plain numeral rather than a term of praise. Its flatness is the point: the statement is offered as a fact to be registered, not as a slogan to be admired.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan society ran on rank held between clans, and rank was maintained in public through hospitality, poetry, feuds and the guardianship of the sanctuary. To accept a message that levelled that order was to accept a demotion in front of everyone who mattered. Several early reports describe men who found the message credible in private and could not bear the loss of standing in public. The word for arrogance in this ayah describes that exact situation.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for the denying heart occurs nowhere else in the Quran. The declaration that opens it, that your god is one god, appears in six places; three of those put it inside an instruction to the Prophet to say it. Only here is it followed straight away by an account of why people refuse it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Denial is diagnosed rather than argued with. By putting the refusal in the heart and naming pride beside it, the passage says that the obstacle to belief is often not intellectual, and it declines to treat every objection as a question deserving an answer. That cuts both ways. It also means the remedy the Quran offers for such refusal is not a better proof but a change in what the person is willing to be.

crossReferences.why: Describes those who behave arrogantly on earth being turned away from the signs themselves.
Says God seals the heart of every arrogant tyrant, linking the same two conditions in reverse order.
States the identical declaration of one God, followed there by the names of mercy rather than by denial.

studies.applyIt: Bring to mind an idea you dismissed quickly and recently. Ask yourself one narrow question about it: would accepting it have cost you anything in front of other people. You are not obliged to change your view. The passage is only pointing out that the answer to that question is often the real reason, and that most of us never check.

studies.title: Legends Of The Ancients
studies.meaning: Two ayat, and the join between them is the interesting part. The first says God knows what people hide and what they announce, and adds that He has no love for the self-important. The second gives an example of announcing: asked what their Lord has sent down, they answer that it is old stories. Commentators note that the reply is not an argument but a way of closing the subject, and that the previous ayah has already named what is being concealed underneath it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The question in the second ayah reflects a real situation, since pilgrims arriving for the seasonal markets asked residents about the man preaching among them, and the Meccan leadership had an interest in the answer given. Classical sources describe deliberate efforts to shape what visitors heard. Whether or not a particular occasion lies behind this ayah, the exchange it records was an ordinary one during the pilgrimage months.

keyTerms.note: A fixed expression that opens a sentence with certainty, close to saying there is no escaping this. Grammarians have long debated how it is built, while agreeing on what it does.
A plural for things set down in lines, which is how the root also gives the word for writing. The charge is that the material is copied from older books rather than newly received.
The earlier generations. Attached to the word for tales it dates the material and dismisses it in one move, since what is old is being treated as already answered.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca ran an annual market season around the pilgrimage, when tribes arrived to trade, recite poetry and settle disputes. News moved through those weeks faster than at any other time, and reputations were made and destroyed in them. A visitor who asked about the new preaching would get the answer the person he asked wanted him to carry home. Controlling that answer was worth real effort to men whose position depended on the sanctuary.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase translated as legends of the ancients occurs exactly nine times in the Quran, always in the mouths of opponents and never in a narrative voice. It is one of the few objections the Quran quotes verbatim more than a handful of times, spread across surahs from the earliest Meccan period to the latest, which shows how durable the charge was.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Setting divine knowledge of the hidden beside a dismissive public answer makes a specific point: the sentence people say is not the whole of what they think, and both are known. That protects the reader from taking stated objections at face value, including their own. The passage also declines to argue with the charge of borrowed stories, and the surah's answer to it comes later, in the form of more material rather than a defence.

crossReferences.why: Quotes the same accusation at length and answers that the One who knows the secret sent it down.
Records the identical phrase as the reaction of a man who hears the verses recited to him.
Puts the same question to a different group in this surah and reports the opposite answer.

studies.applyIt: Listen for the phrase you use to end a conversation you do not want to have. Everyone has one, and it usually sounds like a judgement while doing the work of a door. Catch yourself using it once this week and, instead of finishing the sentence, ask the person one real question. You can still disagree afterwards. You will simply have disagreed with something.

studies.title: Loads Carried Whole
studies.meaning: The image is freight. Those who dismissed the message will carry their own burdens complete, with nothing deducted, and alongside them a share of the burdens of people they turned away without knowledge. The commentators are careful about the second clause: it adds weight to the misleaders without lifting any from those misled, since the wording says some of their loads, not their loads. Responsibility is doubled at one end rather than transferred.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following directly on the answer that the revelation was old stories. This ayah states the consequence of giving that answer publicly. The classical commentators connect it to the men who met arriving pilgrims and warned them off, since a private opinion becomes another person's obstacle at the moment it is broadcast, which is the exact situation the ayah describes.

keyTerms.note: The word for a heavy pack, used of the loads carried in war and by animals. Applying it to wrongdoing turns guilt into freight, which is weighed and carried rather than felt.
An emphatic addition. The point of it is that nothing is quietly written off in transit, which forestalls the hope that some of a load might be lost between here and the weighing.
Attached to those being misled rather than to the misleaders. It marks them as people who did not know enough to judge, which is what makes turning them away a weight worth counting.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Caravan life gave the metaphor its edge. Loads were weighed at departure, and a driver was answerable for what he carried and for anything added to his animal by arrangement. Overloading a camel on a long stage ruined it, and everyone in a trading town had watched a beast go down under weight. The ayah uses a commercial vocabulary its first hearers used every week, and applies it to speech.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase this ayah uses, burdens carried in full, appears nowhere else in the Quran. The same surah later returns to the picture of weight in a different register, and elsewhere the Quran states plainly that no bearer carries another's load, which is why classical commentators read the addition here as extra weight for misleading rather than as guilt moved from one person to another.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two principles are held together that look opposed. No one carries another's burden, and yet leading others astray adds to your own. The resolution is that influence is itself an act, so what is added is the misleader's own doing rather than someone else's debt reassigned. This makes speech consequential in a specific way. What you say about a matter you have not examined becomes part of your own account once it reaches someone who cannot check it.

crossReferences.why: States the principle this ayah must be read against, that no bearer of burdens bears another's.
Reports the same offer to carry others' sins and answers it with the same doubling of weight.
Shows the burdens being carried on the back on the day the reckoning arrives unexpectedly.

studies.applyIt: Think of an opinion you have passed on that you never actually checked. Not a lie, just something you repeated because it sounded right and it was easy. Find the person you said it to and correct it, briefly and without ceremony. The passage is concerned with what happens to a claim after it leaves you, and that is the only part still within reach.

studies.title: The Roof Came Down
studies.meaning: Earlier peoples schemed, and the answer came at their building from underneath. God took the structure from its foundations and the roof fell on them from above, and the punishment reached them from a direction they were not watching. Commentators read the building both as an actual structure in the stories of past nations and as a figure for a scheme, since a plot is something constructed. Either way the point is the direction: the danger was below the part they were defending.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and pointed. The surah has just described people who dismissed the message publicly and turned others away; this ayah tells them the pattern is old and how it usually ends. It names no nation, which the commentators take as deliberate, since the audience knew the ruined sites along their own trade routes and could supply examples without being told which one was meant.

keyTerms.note: Planning carried out in secret, with the sense of turning someone aside from what they intend. It is not a moral word by itself; the Quran uses the same root of God's response to such planning.
The part of a building that sits in the ground, from a root meaning to sit. Attacking a structure there rather than at the walls is what makes the collapse total instead of partial.
A verb for fine awareness, from the same root as the word for a hair and the word for a poet. It names the alertness that catches small signals, and says even that failed here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Building in Arabia meant dry stone and mud brick on shallow footings, and undermining a wall was a known way to bring a structure down without touching its face. Travellers on the northern routes passed the abandoned rock-cut dwellings of earlier peoples and the ruins of towns the caravan roads no longer served. Collapsed roofs were not a metaphor to that audience. They were a landscape feature on the way to Syria.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for foundations appears in only two places in the Quran. Here, where God takes a building away from them, and in surah 2, where Abraham and Ishmael are described raising the foundations of the House in Mecca. The same architectural term marks the one structure that is raised and the one that is pulled out from underneath.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah says something precise about how consequences arrive. Not by overpowering a defence, but by removing the assumption the defence was built on, and from a direction outside the plotter's attention. That describes a limit on human planning that no amount of cleverness closes, since the flaw is in what the planner did not think to consider. The passage does not present this as unfairness. It presents it as the shape events have when they are answered.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for foundations of the House that Abraham raises, the opposite motion to this one.
Describes a scheme so great that mountains might move by it, and says God holds the answer.
Shows a plot answered by a plot the schemers did not perceive, ending in their own ruin.

studies.applyIt: Take a plan you are confident about and spend five minutes on a single question: what am I assuming that I have never checked. Not the risks you have already listed, which are the walls. The thing underneath them. Write down one answer, even a weak one. This passage is about the part of a structure nobody inspects because it is not visible.

studies.title: Where Are My Associates
studies.meaning: A scene rather than a statement. Disgrace comes first, then a question put by God with an edge in it: where are the partners you used to take My side against. The word for that disputing implies choosing an opposing camp. No answer is recorded from the people questioned. Instead a second group speaks, described only as those who were given knowledge, and their verdict is short. The silence of the accused is where the commentators put the weight.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following the ayat on schemes that collapsed from the foundations. The surah has been arguing that consequences arrive from unexpected directions, and this moves the argument to its final scene. The people addressed had spent years defending the standing of the Kaaba's idols in public argument, which is the activity the question names, and the ayah pictures the moment that argument is asked to produce its subject.

keyTerms.note: From a root for public shame rather than private guilt. The humiliation described is social, which fits a group whose position rested on standing among people who are all present.

keyTerms.gloss: you used to oppose, take sides
keyTerms.note: From a root meaning a side or a split, so the verb pictures putting yourself on the far bank from someone. It describes not merely disagreeing but forming a party against.

The noun of the same root as the opening verb, repeated within a single ayah. Repeating it in the mouths of the knowledgeable makes their verdict an echo of the sentence rather than an addition to it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public dispute was a Meccan skill. Cases, feuds and reputations were settled in the assembly beside the sanctuary, and a man who could hold a position in front of the clans held real power. Poets were retained as weapons in those exchanges. To be shamed in that assembly cost a family for a generation. The ayah takes the whole apparatus of standing before a crowd and reuses it, with a different crowd and a different questioner.
studies.didYouKnow: The question at the centre of this ayah, asking where My associates are, is put in four places in the Quran, and in two of them the reply is that no witness is left. The verb describing what the accused used to do, taking a side against, occurs in this form nowhere else, and the ayah uses the root for disgrace twice in one sentence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are established. Judgement includes exposure, not only penalty, so what is settled is partly a matter of public record. And the possessive in the phrase about associates is pointed: they are called God's associates, the ones assigned to Him by other people, which quietly says that the arrangement never existed except in human speech. Knowledge is then given the last word in the scene, which places understanding rather than force at the close.

crossReferences.why: Puts nearly the same question, calling for the associates that people used to claim.
Asks where the partners are and records the reply that no witness remains among them.
Shows those given knowledge recognising the revelation as truth, the same group speaking here.

studies.applyIt: Think of a position you have defended more often than you have examined. Say out loud what it actually commits you to, in one plain sentence, with nothing rhetorical in it. Most positions survive that. Some do not, and it is better to find out now than to discover it while someone is waiting for your answer.

studies.title: The Surrender Offered Too Late
studies.meaning: The moment of death is described as a negotiation that fails. Angels arrive, and the people being taken offer submission along with a denial: we were doing no wrong. The reply is a single word of contradiction, followed by the statement that God knows what they were doing. Commentators note that the surrender itself is not refused for being a surrender; it is refused because it arrives attached to a lie. The gates named afterwards are for the self-important.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a passage that sets two deaths side by side, this one and the one two ayat later. The surah has been describing people whose refusal was tied to social standing rather than to evidence, and it now follows them past the point where standing is worth anything. Nothing here is tied to a named occasion; the commentators read it as the general end of the attitude the surah has been describing.

keyTerms.note: The word for laying down arms and accepting terms, from the same root as peace. Offering it at this point is a military gesture made after the outcome is already decided.
A particle used only to overturn a negative statement. Arabic has a separate word for ordinary agreement; this one exists specifically to answer a denial with a contradiction.
From a root meaning to stay put. It names a place of long residence rather than a stop, which is why it carries weight in a sentence about something without end.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Between tribes, a losing party could throw down its weapons and ask for terms, and the customs around that were exact: what could still be claimed, who guaranteed safety, what a defeated group had to concede. Timing was everything, since an offer made before a rout could save a clan and one made after it usually could not. The passage borrows those conventions and applies them to a moment when the terms are no longer being set by either side.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the one four lines later form a matched pair. The phrase describing those whom the angels take occurs in exactly two places in the Quran, both here in surah 16, and the two are identical up to the single word that describes the state of the person dying: wronging themselves in one, wholesome in the other. Everything else in the two sentences diverges from that word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage draws a line at the moment of death rather than at the moment of judgement, which places the deadline earlier than a reader might expect. What is refused is not repentance but a claim of innocence offered in place of it, and the distinction matters: the denial is what fails, not the lateness alone. Behind it stands the assumption that the record is not open to revision by the person who made it.

crossReferences.why: States plainly that repentance offered when death arrives is not the repentance being asked for.
Shows belief professed at the sight of punishment and says it never benefited anyone before.
Repeats the same gesture of offering surrender in this surah, at the reckoning rather than at death.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between an apology and a defence dressed as one. Most of us make the second and hear ourselves making the first. Pick a recent example and rewrite it in your head with the explanation removed entirely. Whatever is left is the actual apology. If nothing is left, that is worth knowing before it matters more.

studies.title: They Will Say, Goodness
studies.meaning: The same question asked earlier in the surah is put to a different group, and the answer is one word: goodness. Where the first group had classified the revelation as old material, this one describes what it does. The sentence then widens past the answer into a promise with two halves, good in this world for those who do good, and a better home after it. The comparison is made without disparaging the first half.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The question reflects the season when tribes came to Mecca for trade and pilgrimage and asked residents about the new preaching, and the surah has already recorded the dismissive reply given by some. This ayah supplies the other reply that visitors would have heard, from the smaller group who had accepted the message, which is why the two answers are placed six ayat apart in the same chapter.

keyTerms.note: A single word answering a question about content with a judgement about worth. It also serves as the comparative, so the same word returns later in the ayah meaning better, tying the answer to the promise.

From a root meaning beauty as well as goodness, and carrying the sense of doing something well rather than merely doing the right thing. The reward named uses the same root, so the return matches the act.
The word for a household's dwelling and the courtyard it encloses, not a house as a building. Applied to the hereafter it suggests belonging and settlement rather than accommodation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: For an Arab of that period a home meant a compound of related families with its animals, its dependants and its guests, and to be without one was to be exposed. Exile from a clan's protection could be a death sentence, since no one was obliged to avenge or shelter you. The word the ayah chooses for the hereafter is that word, so the promise is not of a better building but of belonging somewhere permanently.
studies.didYouKnow: The question asked here, what your Lord has sent down, appears in exactly two places in the Quran, and both are in this surah, six ayat apart. It is put to two different groups and receives two answers of one word each. Nowhere else does the Quran stage the same question twice with opposite replies in a single chapter.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The good of this world is not treated as a consolation or a trap. It is granted first, plainly, and only then compared with something greater, which keeps the comparison from turning into contempt for the present. The passage also connects what a person says about revelation with how they act, since those who answered goodness and those who do good are described in the same breath without the link being spelled out.

crossReferences.why: Puts the identical question to a different group in this surah and records the opposite answer.
States the underlying principle, that the reward of doing well is nothing but doing well.
Promises good in this world to those who do good, and adds that the earth is spacious.

studies.applyIt: Someone will ask you this week what you think of something you value. Answer in one sentence about what it does rather than what it is. The reply in this ayah is a single word and it describes an effect, not a category. Categories end conversations. Effects invite the next question, which is usually the one worth having.

studies.title: Gardens Of Perpetual Residence
studies.meaning: The home promised a line earlier is now named. Gardens of settled dwelling, entered rather than glimpsed, with water running underneath them, and then a clause that stops describing and hands the description over: they have there whatever they wish. Commentators note the shift from a list to an open category, since anything specified would be smaller than the promise. The ayah closes by attributing the whole arrangement to a single act of recompense.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Descriptions of the garden in the Meccan surahs are short and concrete, drawing on what an audience in a dry valley would recognise as luxury: shade, running water, permanence. The elaboration found in later passages is not here. The ayah is a direct continuation of the one before it, supplying the content of the better home that had just been promised without description.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to stay in a place, which also gives Arabic the word for a mine, a thing fixed where it lies. Commentators differ over whether it is also a proper name for a particular garden.
A verb of continuous motion, in a tense that keeps the action ongoing rather than completed. Running water, as opposed to stored water, was the mark of a place that would not fail.
From a root for settling an account in full. It presents the garden as a discharge of what is owed rather than a gift, which the commentators balance against the many ayat calling it grace.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In Arabia a garden meant an enclosure with a water source, and the water was the whole of it. Wells and cisterns had to be lifted from, and a spring that ran on its own was rare and valuable enough to define a settlement's history. Ta'if and the oases north of Mecca were famous precisely for this. Shade, which the ayah implies rather than states, was the second scarce thing, and the two together were what wealth bought.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase used here for gardens of perpetual residence occurs in eleven places across the Quran, in both Meccan and Medinan surahs, which makes it the most frequently repeated of all the garden names. The next most common, the gardens of bliss, appears eight times. The clause about having whatever one wishes is far rarer, and commentators treat it as the widest description given.
studies.theologicalSignificance: By ending the description with an open clause, the passage refuses to fix a ceiling on what is promised, which does real theological work: it prevents the garden from being reduced to the particular pleasures a given culture happens to prize. Setting reward language beside a picture of permanence also answers the anxiety underneath most human striving, which is not that good things do not exist but that they do not last.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same clause about having whatever they wish, and calls it a promise to be asked for.
Names the same gardens and adds the entry of righteous relatives and the greeting of the angels.
Repeats the open promise, extending it to whatever the soul desires and whatever is called for.

studies.applyIt: Write down what you would actually ask for if the clause in this ayah were addressed to you. Not the answer you think is expected. The exercise is uncomfortable because most lists come back short and oddly specific, and noticing that is the point. What you would ask for tells you what you have been organising your week around.

studies.title: Peace Be Upon You
studies.meaning: The second of two deaths described in this stretch, and the mirror of the first. The angels arrive again, and the people they come for are described with one word meaning wholesome or in good state. Commentators read it of the condition of the soul and, in some reports, of the ease of the departure itself. There is no negotiation here because nothing is being contested. The angels speak first, with a greeting, and the entry is attributed to what the person had been doing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and deliberately placed. The surah has just shown a death that goes badly, then the reward promised to those who kept their duty, and it now returns to the same moment for the other group. Nothing suggests a specific occasion. The classical commentators treat the pairing as the surah's way of making the two outcomes comparable by describing them at the same instant rather than at the judgement.

keyTerms.note: A word covering what is clean, pleasant and fit for use, applied to food, soil and speech. Used of people at death it suggests something sound rather than merely blameless.
The ordinary greeting, offered here unchanged. Its plainness is the point: the first words spoken are the same ones exchanged between neighbours, which locates the moment inside familiar courtesy.

A small preposition doing large work. It attaches entry to prior action, and the commentators read it alongside the many statements that entry is by mercy, treating deeds as a cause God appointed rather than a price.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arrival was a formal thing in that society. A traveller reaching a camp called out a greeting before approaching, and the answer determined whether he was a guest or a threat, since being received meant food, shelter and protection for three days by custom. Hospitality was the strongest social obligation there was. The ayah has the angels use exactly that formula, which places the newly dead in the position of a guest expected rather than a stranger arriving.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the one four lines earlier open with the identical phrase about those whom the angels take, and that phrase occurs nowhere else in the Quran. The two sentences separate on a single word: one group is described as wronging themselves, the other as wholesome. The word chosen for the second group appears in the whole Quran only twice.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing a greeting at the moment of death changes what the moment is. It is presented as a reception rather than a seizure, and the courtesy is initiated by the arriving party, which reverses the ordinary anxiety about being met by an unknown authority. The description of the person as wholesome also matters: what is commended is a state, something a life settles into, rather than a tally of acts, though the acts are named in the same sentence.

crossReferences.why: Has angels descend on those who stood firm, telling them not to fear or grieve.
Addresses the settled soul directly at the same moment, calling it back to its Lord.
Gives the matching sentence in this surah for those taken in the opposite state.

studies.applyIt: Greet one person today whom you usually pass without speaking. A neighbour, someone at the same bus stop, whoever is behind the counter. Say the words properly rather than in passing. This ayah puts an ordinary greeting at the most serious moment there is, which suggests the small courtesies are not a lesser category of thing.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: What Are They Waiting For
studies.meaning: A question with only one answer available. If the evidence already given is not enough, what remains is the arrival of the angels or of the command itself, and by then the matter is closed. The passage then notes that earlier peoples did exactly the same, and forestalls the obvious complaint: God did not wrong them. What reached them was the consequence of their own acts, and the thing they had treated as a joke closed over them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following the two death scenes. The demand for a visible sign was a real and repeated Meccan objection, recorded in several surahs, and the classical sources describe specific challenges to produce angels or a punishment on demand. This ayah does not answer the demand. It points out what granting it would mean, and then observes that the pattern of asking is older than the people asking.

keyTerms.note: The verb covers both waiting and watching, so the sentence pictures people scanning for something rather than merely delaying. The English question loses the sense of eyes on the horizon.
A verb used of something surrounding a person on every side, with no sense of an impact. What was mocked does not strike; it settles over them, which is why translators reach for engulfed.
A form implying seeking amusement at someone's expense, done for an audience. It names a social act rather than a private opinion, which is why the response described is equally public.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mockery was a weapon with rules. Satirical verse was composed to order, memorised and carried between tribes, and a well-made line could damage a clan's marriage prospects and trade for years. Poets who specialised in it were feared and paid. The early years in Mecca were fought partly on that ground, which is why ridicule appears so often in these surahs as the characteristic form of opposition rather than argument.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb translated as engulfed occurs in this past-tense form six times in the Quran, and in every one of them the subject is the same: what people used to ridicule, closing around them. It is never given any other subject in that form. Classical commentators note that the Quran reserves the word for the moment when mockery returns on the one who offered it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The clause denying wrong is doing careful work. It rules out the reading in which consequence is imposed from outside as an added penalty, and describes it instead as the deeds themselves arriving. That keeps justice and mercy in the same frame, since nothing is added to what a person made. The rhetorical question at the start makes a further point: a sign large enough to compel belief would arrive at the moment when belief no longer costs anything, and so would not be belief.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same demand by saying that when a sign arrives, faith will no longer benefit anyone.
States the same denial, that God does not wrong people, but people wrong themselves.
Uses the identical verb for what people mocked closing around them once the delay ends.

studies.applyIt: Find the thing you are waiting for before you make a change: a sign, a clearer moment, one more piece of information. Name it exactly, then ask whether you would actually act on it or move the marker again. Most people discover they have moved it before. That is worth knowing today rather than in the version of this where the waiting has run out.

studies.title: Had God Willed, We Would Not
studies.meaning: An argument is quoted rather than paraphrased. Since God is able to prevent anything, the fact that we and our fathers served other objects, and declared certain things off limits, must be what He wanted. The Quran gives no direct rebuttal here. It observes that earlier peoples argued the same way, and then closes with a question about the messenger's job, which is to deliver clearly. Commentators read the omission as pointed: the argument is not answered because it was never being used to find the truth.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The second half of the quoted speech refers to a real Meccan practice, since certain animals and crops were set aside from ordinary use by custom, dedicated in ways the surah addresses elsewhere. The argument recorded is therefore not abstract. It was a defence of an existing system of religious observance, and the ayah reproduces the reasoning its holders actually used to justify inherited practice.

keyTerms.note: From the root that gives sanctuary and the sacred precinct. The verb means to place something outside ordinary use, which is what the Meccans did with certain animals dedicated to their objects of worship.
The noun for getting a message all the way to its destination, used of couriers. It defines the messenger's task as transmission complete, and stops there without extending to results.
An active form, so it means not merely clear in itself but clarifying. The delivery is required to make the matter plain, which sets a standard for the messenger while leaving the response to others.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Pre-Islamic Arabia had an elaborate system of dedicated animals, camels marked and released from work, produce apportioned between the sanctuary and the household. These customs were inherited, defended as ancestral, and enforced by community pressure rather than by any text. Changing them meant breaking with fathers and grandfathers by name, in a society where lineage was the main form of memory. The argument this ayah quotes was in part a defence of that inheritance.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase describing the messenger's duty as clear delivery occurs seven times in the Quran, and two of those are in this surah, at this ayah and again near its end. In most of the other places it follows an instruction to obey; here alone it follows a quoted argument, and functions as a limit on what the messenger is answerable for.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a boundary rather than settling the question of divine will and human action. Both are affirmed elsewhere in the Quran without being reconciled into a system, and the classical commentators preserve that tension rather than resolving it. What this ayah rules out is a particular use of the doctrine: turning God's power into an excuse after the fact. The test it implies is practical, whether the reasoning is applied to future choices or only to past ones.

crossReferences.why: Quotes the same argument almost word for word and calls it conjecture rather than knowledge.
Records the identical excuse, that the Merciful would not have let them worship these.
Repeats the clause about clear delivery at the close of this surah, in a different setting.

studies.applyIt: Catch one explanation you give for something you keep doing, and test it the way this ayah does. Ask whether you would accept the same reasoning as a guide to a decision you have not made yet. If it only ever works backwards, it is not a reason. It is an account, and knowing which one you are holding is the whole of the exercise.

studies.title: A Messenger In Every Community
studies.meaning: One sentence covers all of history. Every community received a messenger carrying two instructions, one positive and one negative, and the outcomes divided. Some God guided, and on others misguidance came due. The reader is then told to travel and look at what happened to those who denied. The second ayah turns to the Prophet's own eagerness for his people, and sets a limit on it that the commentators handle carefully, since the sentence does not say his concern is misplaced.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, at a point where the message had been public for years and the response had settled into a pattern. The instruction to travel and look was literal for this audience: the caravan routes north passed ruined settlements, and Meccan traders made that journey twice a year. The ayah asks them to read something they already saw twice annually as evidence rather than as scenery.

keyTerms.note: A people bound by something shared, not necessarily by descent or territory. Using it here makes the claim broad: wherever a group with a common life existed, a messenger came to it.
From a root meaning to overflow a limit. It covers idols, tyrants and anything given the obedience owed to God, so the word is defined by the position taken rather than the thing itself.
A verb of intense wanting, used of greed elsewhere. Applied to the Prophet's desire for his people's guidance, it describes an appetite rather than a duty, which is what the ayah goes on to bound.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The road north from Mecca to Syria passed the rock-cut tombs of an earlier people at al-Hijr and the traces of settlements the trade had abandoned. Merchants camped near these places and the stories attached to them circulated as common knowledge. Southward lay the ruins of the dam country in Yemen. Nobody in the audience needed a library to check the claim in this ayah. They needed only to remember the last journey they had made.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for what must be avoided appears in eight places in the Quran, and it is not a name for any particular idol. Lexicographers derive it from a verb meaning to exceed a boundary, which is why classical commentators apply it to anything obeyed in God's place, including a person or a custom, rather than to statues alone.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The claim that every community received a messenger has consequences the commentators drew out: no people is left without address, and the message given is always the same pair of instructions, so difference between traditions is not difference at the root. The second ayah then separates concern from responsibility. The Prophet is not told to care less, only that the outcome is not his to produce, which distinguishes obligation from result in a way the tradition applied widely.

crossReferences.why: States the same universality, that no community passed without a warner sent to it.
Gives the identical two-part message to every messenger before, worship Me and nothing else.
Addresses the same grief over those who refuse, in stronger terms, and gently checks it.

studies.applyIt: Take the person whose choices you have been trying hardest to change. Write down the part of it that is your work and the part that is not, in two short lists. Then act only on the first for a week. This passage does not ask you to care less. It asks you to stop paying for an outcome that was never on your side of the line.

studies.title: Sworn With Their Strongest Oaths
studies.meaning: The denial of resurrection is reported not as an opinion but as an oath, and the phrase used means the most binding form of swearing available. Commentators note the oddity of invoking God to deny what God has undertaken. The answer overturns it with a single particle and then restates the matter as a promise binding upon Him, which shifts the ground: the question is no longer what is possible but what has been undertaken. The closing clause explains the disagreement as ignorance rather than defiance.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Bodily resurrection was the single hardest element of the message for its first audience, and the Quran returns to it constantly in the Meccan surahs. Classical sources report men bringing crumbled bone to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) as an argument. Swearing by God while rejecting the resurrection was not a contradiction to them, since they acknowledged a creator God and denied only that He would raise the dead.

keyTerms.note: From a root for exertion to the limit. Attached to oaths it names the most solemn formula a person had, the one reserved for matters where their word had to carry alone.
A particle whose only job is to reverse a negative. Set against the heaviest oath in the language, its brevity is the response: no counter-oath is offered, only a contradiction and then a statement.

Placed with a word meaning binding upon, so the sentence describes God as having obliged Himself. The commentators note that the obligation is self-imposed, which is the only sense in which anything is due from Him.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a society without courts or written contracts, an oath was the instrument that settled disputes. Ownership of a well, the paternity of a child, a debt, a killing: all could turn on a formula sworn in front of witnesses, and there were graded oaths for graded matters. A man known to have sworn falsely lost the ability to transact. Reaching for the strongest oath available signalled that a claim was being staked at maximum cost.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for the most solemn form of swearing occurs five times in the Quran, and in every one of them it introduces something the speakers turn out to be wrong about or fail to keep. None of the five is ever spoken by someone whose oath holds. Classical commentators observe that the Quran repeatedly pairs the heaviest available oath with the weakest available position.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply moves the argument from capacity to commitment. Resurrection is not defended here as something God could do but as something He has undertaken to do, which makes the issue one of reliability rather than power. The last clause then declines to call the deniers liars, saying instead that most people do not know. That distinction between ignorance and defiance runs through the Quran's treatment of unbelief, and it changes what response is appropriate.

crossReferences.why: Records the same oath denying resurrection and answers with an instruction to say otherwise.
Answers the argument from crumbled bones by pointing back to the first origination.
Uses the identical phrase for the strongest oaths, sworn there over a demanded sign.

studies.applyIt: Notice how hard you swear when you are least sure. Most people raise the intensity of a claim exactly where the evidence thins, and it is audible if you listen for it in yourself. Next time you catch the phrase that means you are staking everything on something, stop and ask what you would actually accept as proof against it.

studies.title: Be, And It Is
studies.meaning: Two reasons are given for the resurrection just affirmed. It will settle what people disagreed about, and it will show those who refused that they were saying something false. Neither reason is about punishment; both are about the record being made clear. Then the difficulty is dismissed in one line. When God intends a thing, He says be to it, and it is. Commentators note that the sentence removes any question of effort or material, which was the whole objection.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, answering the oath recorded two ayat earlier that God will not raise anyone who dies. The Meccan objection was practical rather than philosophical: bones decay, and nobody had seen the reverse. This pair of ayat answers first by explaining what the raising is for, and then by locating the difficulty where the objectors had not thought to look, in their assumption that making requires a process.

keyTerms.gloss: so that He may make clear
keyTerms.note: From the root for separating one thing from another, which is how Arabic builds the idea of clarity. What is promised is not a verdict imposed but a distinction made visible.

A form suggesting mutual difference, people taking turns behind each other. It covers honest disagreement as well as dispute, which is why the promise here is of clarification rather than of sentence.
The shortest imperative in the language, two letters. The commentators observe that the brevity is the argument, since a command needing no elaboration describes a making that needs no material.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything the audience made, they made from something. A tent was woven from hair that had been sheared, spun and dyed; a well was dug; a sword was traded for or beaten out of imported iron. Craft in that world was visible and slow, and it was the model people reasoned from. Bones that had gone to dust offered no material to work with, which is exactly why the objection felt decisive to the people making it.
studies.didYouKnow: The command translated as be, followed by and it is, occurs in eight places in the Quran. Three of them appear in passages about Jesus, two in passages about the origination of the heavens and the earth, and three, including this one, in passages about giving life and raising the dead. The same two-word formula covers the beginning of the world, a birth, and the end.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming clarification as the purpose of the resurrection makes it an act of truth-telling before it is an act of judgement, which reframes what the day is for. The second ayah then places God's action outside the category of work altogether. This has a consequence the commentators drew: since nothing is easier or harder for such an act, arguments from difficulty do not apply, and what remains to discuss is only whether the thing was undertaken.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same formula immediately after answering the argument from decayed bones.
Applies the identical words to the origination of the heavens and the earth without a model.
Uses the same command for the creation of Jesus, comparing it to the making of Adam from dust.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have decided is impossible, and separate the two things hiding inside that word. One is that you cannot do it. The other is that it cannot be done. Write which of the two you actually mean. The passage is about the second kind, and most of what we call impossible turns out to be the first.

studies.title: Settled In A Good Place
