studies.meaning: A promise made to people who left. The clause specifying that they emigrated for God's sake after being wronged sets two conditions at once, a motive and a prior injury, and the commentators treat both as load-bearing. What is promised is a settling, in this world, in something good, and then a larger reward afterwards. The sentence closes with a conditional half-line that is left hanging: if only they knew. The subject of that clause is disputed among the commentators.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is Meccan, but many classical commentators hold this ayah and the one after it to belong to a later stage. Some read them of the migration to Abyssinia during the Meccan years, when a group left to escape persecution; others hold them to be among the Medinan ayat of this surah and read them of the emigration to Medina. The reports differ, and the tradition preserves both readings side by side rather than settling on one.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to cut off or abandon, so the word carries severance rather than travel. It names leaving people and a place behind, which is why it also gives the word for parting speech.
A verb for assigning someone a dwelling and putting them in it, doubled here with emphatic markers. The word implies being housed by another's arrangement rather than finding a place yourself.
Deliberately unspecified. Commentators list safety, provision, honour and victory among the readings, and note that leaving the noun open lets the promise fit whatever the emigrant actually lacked.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Leaving your tribe was close to unthinkable. Protection came from kin, and a man outside that network had no one to avenge him, no one to stand surety for a debt, and no claim on hospitality beyond the customary three days. Emigrants arrived somewhere as dependants with no standing at all. The word this ayah uses for settling them is the word for being given a place by someone else, which is exactly the position such people were in.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase used here, emigrating for God's sake, occurs nowhere else in the Quran. Other passages speak of emigrating in God's way or for His cause, using a different preposition. Classical commentators note the difference, reading this construction as naming God as the whole object of the move rather than the direction of it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The promise is deliberately double, and the order matters: something good here first, and only then the greater reward. That refuses a purely deferred consolation, which would have been the easier thing to offer people who had lost houses and trade. The trailing clause about knowledge then does something quieter. It suggests the difficulty of the situation is not only material but epistemic, since what would make the loss bearable is information the sufferer does not yet have.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same promise to those who emigrated and were then killed or died on the way.
Describes the earth as containing many a refuge and abundance for one who emigrates.
Tells believing servants that God's earth is spacious, so worship Him wherever you are.

studies.applyIt: If you have moved away from somewhere, for whatever reason, name one good thing that came from the move that you could not have arranged yourself. Not to balance the ledger, and not instead of what was lost. This ayah puts the worldly good first and does not pretend it settles anything. Naming it accurately is different from being consoled by it.

studies.title: Ask Those Who Know
studies.meaning: The first line finishes the previous sentence by naming what those emigrants did: they held out, and they relied on their Lord. The two are given in that order, endurance first and reliance second, which the commentators read as describing a sequence rather than two names for one thing. The second line turns to an objection about the messenger being an ordinary man, and answers it by pointing outward: put the question to people who have the relevant knowledge.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is Meccan, though a number of classical commentators hold the preceding ayat about emigration to belong to a later stage. The objection answered in the second line was a live Meccan complaint, that a genuine messenger would be an angel rather than a man from a known family. The people directed to are generally understood as those familiar with earlier scriptures, who could confirm that every previous messenger had also been human.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to confine or restrain. The word is closer to holding a position than to accepting a fate, which is why it also gives the word for binding an animal in one place.
From the root for appointing an agent to act on your behalf. The grammar implies handing a matter over after doing your part, not instead of doing it, which is how the commentators read it.

Covers remembrance, mention and a revealed book. Attached to people it names those who carry the earlier revelations in memory, which is why the phrase is usually read as a direction to prior scripture.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia had Jewish and Christian communities within reach, in Yathrib, in Yemen and along the northern trade roads, and Meccan merchants dealt with them regularly. Monks and rabbis were consulted as a matter of course on questions about earlier prophets, and stories from those scriptures circulated in Arabic by word of mouth. Directing an objector to ask them was practical advice, not a rhetorical gesture. The people meant could be found on the next journey north.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction to ask the people of the reminder occurs in exactly two places in the Quran, here and in surah 21, and the two ayat are nearly identical: both begin by saying that only men were sent before, both add that they received revelation, and both close with the same conditional about not knowing. The pairing is one of the closest verbal repetitions between two surahs.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Answering a theological objection by directing people to inquire is unusual, and the commentators note what it assumes: that the record of earlier prophecy is public, checkable, and consistent with the claim being made. It treats revelation as continuous rather than unprecedented. The two words in the first line establish something separate, that reliance on God is compatible with strain, since patience is named as the thing being done while the reliance is going on.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction in nearly identical words and adds that those sent ate food.
Answers the same objection by noting that every messenger before ate and walked in markets.
Sets out what reliance on God is promised to produce, a way out and provision unlooked for.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you have an opinion about but have never asked anyone qualified. Find a person who actually knows and ask them a single question, phrased so it can be answered. This ayah answers a serious objection by telling the objector where to look, which assumes the asking is available. Usually it still is, and we simply do not do it.

studies.title: That You May Clarify
studies.meaning: The ayah completes the sentence begun before it about messengers sent with clear proofs and written scriptures, then turns to the present task. The Reminder was sent down not only to be recited but to be explained, so the messenger's role includes making plain what the revelation says. The commentators take the clarifying to cover both the wording and how it applies. The closing clause shifts the weight back onto the hearers, whose reflection is the purpose of the whole transaction.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah addressed largely to people who denied that an ordinary human being could carry revelation. The preceding ayat answer that objection by pointing to earlier communities who also received men as messengers. This ayah names what those messengers carried and why the present one has been given the same. No specific occasion is reported; it belongs to the sustained Meccan argument about prophecy.

keyTerms.note: A name for the revelation that presents it as recall rather than novelty. The root covers both mentioning aloud and holding in mind, so it names the text and the effect it is meant to have.
An intensive verb for making something distinct and unmistakable. It assumes the text can be misread, and treats explaining it as part of the message rather than an addition to it.
A reflexive form suggesting sustained turning over rather than a single thought. The grammar makes reflection something the hearers do to themselves, which no messenger can do on their behalf.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was a largely oral culture where authority travelled by memory and recitation. A poet or an orator delivered his lines and then, if pressed, explained them. Written scripture belonged to the Jewish and Christian communities to the north, whose scrolls Meccan traders had seen on the Syrian routes. Naming both proofs and written books set this recitation alongside something the caravans already knew existed.
studies.didYouKnow: The word rendered as the Reminder appears twice in a row here. The ayah just before it tells objectors to ask the people of the Reminder, and this one says the Reminder was sent down to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). One term names an older body of scripture and the new revelation within two consecutive lines.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is presented as needing a human interpreter, which places prophecy in explanation as well as in delivery. That rules out a text operating on its own with nobody standing behind it. At the same time the final clause refuses to make understanding automatic. The clarifying is done, and the reflecting is still left to the hearer, so guidance is offered rather than installed.

crossReferences.why: Runs straight into this ayah, naming the people of the Reminder just before the Reminder itself is named.
States that every messenger came in his own people's tongue, which is what makes clarification possible.
Describes a covenant to make scripture clear to people and not to conceal it.

studies.applyIt: Take one ayah you have heard many times and read a short explanation of it this week, from a source you trust. Notice whether the explanation changes anything or only confirms what you had assumed. The last word of this ayah is about reflecting, and reflection needs something to work on besides the sound.

studies.title: Do They Feel Secure
studies.meaning: A question opens a short series of possibilities, each naming a different way ruin could arrive. The commentators note that the schemers are being asked about their confidence rather than about their guilt. Nothing here predicts that any of it will happen. What the question dismantles is the assumption underneath the plotting: that the ground is stable, that consequences announce themselves in advance, and that a plan made in secret can actually be secured.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a period when opposition had moved past argument into organised scheming against the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and those who followed him. The surah has just recalled communities before whose plotting was answered from a direction they had not watched. The classical commentators attach this warning to the general Meccan situation rather than to one named plot, and report no particular occasion.

keyTerms.note: A verb for a plan whose success depends on staying hidden. Across the Quran it usually pairs human scheming with a counter-move, so the word tends to carry its own answer with it.
Used of ground giving way and swallowing whatever stands on it. The image belongs to earthquake and sinkhole rather than to storm or flood, so the danger named comes from below.
From a root for fine, intuitive awareness rather than deliberate knowledge. Denying it says the harm would arrive below the threshold at which they might have sensed it coming.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian trade ran on secrecy. A caravan's route and hour of departure were held close, alliances were negotiated quietly, and a boycott could be agreed before its target heard of it. Meccans had also inherited stories of settlements in the north swallowed or buried, ruins the northern routes actually passed. Ground that opens was not a figure of speech to people who travelled by those sites.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence begun here is not finished within this ayah. It continues through the two that follow, adding alternatives joined by the same short particle for or, and it never states an outcome. Classical commentators read the accumulation itself as the argument: the list is not complete, and its purpose is to show that no direction has been covered.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates security from safety. People are not told they are about to be destroyed. They are told that their sense of being beyond reach has no basis, which makes the target of the warning an inner state rather than an event. It also places the timing and the direction of consequence entirely outside human calculation, and that is what makes scheming, as a way of living, unworkable.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle directly, that only those already losing feel secure from the planning of God.
Narrates a case in which the earth actually caves in, giving this warning a precedent.
Shows human scheming answered by a better plan, which is the pattern this question assumes.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you catch yourself thinking a situation is handled. Not that it will go badly, only that you have counted every direction it could come from. Ask honestly how many of those directions you actually checked. The ayah is not asking you to become anxious. It is asking you to stop treating a plan as a guarantee.

studies.title: Or While In Dread
studies.meaning: Two further possibilities close the series: seizure in the middle of ordinary movement, and seizure while a person is already afraid. Then the sentence turns without warning. Instead of naming a punishment it names God as Gentle and Merciful, and the commentators read that ending as the reason the warning has been issued rather than carried out. Scholars differ over the second phrase, some taking it as gradual loss and others as fear of a coming blow.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is arguing with people who had grown confident that nothing would interrupt their arrangements. These two ayat finish a question begun above and then break its momentum entirely. The classical commentators report no particular occasion, reading the pair as part of the surah's steady alternation between warning and the naming of God's kindness, a rhythm that runs through its Meccan sections.

keyTerms.note: A word for turning back and forth, used of travel and of the ordinary busyness of trade. It places the possible seizure inside routine rather than at some singled-out dramatic moment.
Scholars differ over the sense. Some read a gradual diminishing, others a fear that precedes a blow, and both readings survive in the classical commentaries without either being settled.
A name for tenderness that shrinks from causing hurt. Placed after a list of ways ruin might arrive, it explains why the list stays hypothetical instead of becoming a sentence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A merchant's life was movement: loading before dawn, weeks on the road, settling accounts in a market town, turning round again. Sudden death on the route was common enough that wills were made before departure. So was the slower ruin, a season of raids or collapsed prices eating a family's holdings until nothing remained. Both kinds of ending were familiar, and neither announced itself.
studies.didYouKnow: The two divine names that close this passage, Gentle and Merciful, occur as a pair nine times in the Quran. This surah uses that pair once before, near its opening, where it describes the animals that carry loads to towns people could not otherwise reach. The warning and the kindness are given the same closing vocabulary.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses to let power and tenderness stand as alternatives. The same sentence that lists three ways a life could end without notice finishes by naming God as the one who is gentle, and neither clause softens the other. What the arrangement establishes is that delay is not indifference and not weakness. It is a quality of the one delaying, described here so that it can be relied on.

crossReferences.why: Closes with the identical pair of names, there attached to the animals that carry burdens for people.
Repeats the point that no creature would remain on earth if consequence were not deferred.
Lists directions from which trouble might come, in the same open-ended way this question does.

studies.applyIt: Think of a fear you carry that is about slow loss rather than sudden disaster, the kind that erodes. This passage names that kind separately, which means it is not too small to be taken seriously. Bring that particular fear into your prayer tonight in plain words, and end it with the two names this passage ends with.

studies.title: Shadows Leaning Away
studies.meaning: The argument switches from warning to observation, and asks whether anyone has actually watched. Shadows move. They lean one way in the morning and the other in the afternoon, and the passage reads that movement as prostration. The commentators note that the verb describes a shadow returning, so the daily circuit itself is the act rather than any single position. The closing word says the bowing is not chosen.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the middle of an extended argument that runs from the objections of the deniers to the evidence lying in plain sight. The surah has already used rain, cattle, the sea and the stars in this way. Here it turns to something with no obvious usefulness at all, which is part of the point being made. The classical commentators report no specific occasion for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: A verb for a shadow returning after the sun has moved it. The form suggests repetition, so the prostration described is the whole daily circuit rather than one fixed posture.
A plural used of a single created thing. Commentators read it as the shadow being counted at each hour it occupies, which keeps the emphasis on movement rather than on shape.
A word for being lowered against one's own inclination. It ends the ayah on a submission that is not voluntary, which is what distinguishes what shadows do from what a worshipper does.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Before clocks, a shadow was the instrument. Prayer times, market openings and the hour to move a herd were judged by the length of a man's shadow measured against his own foot, a reading anyone could take anywhere. Travellers found direction by it at midday. Watching shadows was not contemplation for the first hearers. It was the ordinary skill by which a day was divided.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of a small group of ayat that describe things without will as prostrating, and the surah places it immediately before the only prostration marked for recitation in its hundred and twenty-eight ayat. There are fifteen such marks in the whole Quran. A reader following them will bow at the passage that comes next.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prostration is redefined by being extended to things that have no will, and that does two things at once. It says the universe is already in the posture human beings are asked to take, so worship is joining something rather than beginning it. And it makes human prostration distinctive precisely because it can be refused. The shadow has no say in the matter, and the reader does.

crossReferences.why: Says the same of shadows in the mornings and evenings, and carries a prostration mark of its own.
Pairs stars and trees as things that bow, extending the same category in a different direction.
Widens it to a praise offered by everything, which human beings are said not to understand.

studies.applyIt: Step outside once tomorrow around midday and look at your own shadow, then look again in the late afternoon. It will have crossed to the other side. That is all this ayah asks anyone to notice. Spend the thirty seconds it takes rather than agreeing in principle that shadows move.

studies.title: And They Are Not Proud
studies.meaning: The scope widens from shadows to everything that moves in the heavens and on earth, then names the angels separately and says of them that they are not proud. Two short clauses follow: they fear their Lord above them, and they do what they are commanded. Only after all of that does the instruction arrive, and it comes as a prohibition about number. The commentators read the ordering as deliberate rather than incidental.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been building a case from observable creation towards the single claim its audience rejected, and these ayat complete that movement. The address at the end shifts into direct speech reported as God's own words, which the classical commentators treat as a change of register rather than the mark of a new occasion. No particular event is reported for the passage.

keyTerms.note: From a root for treading or crawling. It covers everything that moves under its own power, so the sentence sweeps in animals the audience never considered alongside the angels named next.
A reflexive form meaning to make oneself great. It presents pride as a claim a creature makes about itself, which is why denying it of angels is a statement about accuracy rather than manners.
The dual form. The prohibition is framed against exactly two rather than against many, which commentators read as striking at the idea of a rival at all, since two is the smallest possible plurality.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sanctuary at Mecca held a large number of tribal images, and pilgrimage to it was the city's income. Each tribe kept its own, and the arrangement worked because none of them claimed exclusivity. A household could add a deity without subtracting one. Against that background, a prohibition framed around the number two lands exactly where the practice actually stood.
studies.didYouKnow: The middle ayah of this passage carries one of the fifteen prostration marks in the Quran, and it is the only one in this surah of a hundred and twenty-eight ayat. In many recitation traditions a reader who reaches it stops and prostrates, so a passage about creatures bowing produces an actual bow from the person reading it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Pride is treated as a factual error rather than a flaw of character. The angels are not praised for restraint. They are described as accurate about their own position, which is why the absence of pride sits beside obedience as one condition rather than two. And placing the prohibition after the survey means the oneness of God arrives as the conclusion of an observation, not as a demand issued in advance of one.

crossReferences.why: Describes those near God as free of pride and prostrating, using the same two ideas together.
Adds that the angels never tire of praise, extending the description of them given here.
States the same oneness positively, where this passage states it as a prohibition against two.

studies.applyIt: Notice one place today where you would rather be right than accurate. A small one works better for this. The passage does not describe angels as humble by effort; it describes them as not overstating their position. Try saying out loud, to one person, a sentence that gives up a little of the standing you had claimed.

studies.title: Obedience Owed Without Interruption
studies.meaning: Ownership is stated first, and the second clause draws its conclusion with a single adverb: what is owed to God is owed permanently. The commentators take that word to cover both constancy and inevitability, which rules out an obedience that is seasonal or contractual. The closing question then presses on the practice the hearers actually had, which was distributing their fear among several powers and reserving the largest share for whichever seemed nearest.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the section that began with shadows and reached the prohibition against taking two gods. The question at the end is aimed at people who acknowledged God as creator while spreading their caution among lesser powers. The classical commentators treat the ayah as gathering up the argument rather than answering a particular incident, and they report no occasion for it.

keyTerms.note: The word later comes to mean religion, but its older sense is what a lower party owes a higher one. Reading it as a debt keeps the sentence tied to the ownership clause before it.
From a root for something continuous and also for wearing effort. Commentators give both permanence and obligation, so the word says the debt neither lapses nor pauses at any point.

A verb for taking protective care, which in practice means arranging your life around avoiding something. The question asks what the hearers actually organise themselves around, not what they profess.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fear in that society was practical and distributed. You feared a stronger tribe, a creditor, a season of drought, the displeasure of a shrine's guardians. Protection was bought with alliance and gift, and a man who offended the wrong power lost the safety of the road. Asking whom the hearers feared was asking whose favour their travel and their trade depended on.
studies.didYouKnow: The word rendered here as constant occurs only twice in the Quran, and the other occurrence describes a punishment rather than a duty. The same term for something that does not let up is used once for what is owed to God and once for what awaits those who reject Him, which is a deliberate symmetry.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah derives obligation from ownership rather than from benefit or from threat, and that is a specific move. It means the claim on a person does not rise or fall with how their life is going. It also identifies divided fear as the practical form of associating partners with God, since what a person guards against reveals who they believe holds their outcome more reliably than what they say.

crossReferences.why: Argues from the same premise, that everything already submits, towards the same conclusion about what is owed.
Answers this closing question in the first person, with devotion made deliberately exclusive.
Asks directly whether people are more deserving of a person's fear than God is.

studies.applyIt: Make a short list tonight of the three things you are most careful never to provoke. A person, an institution, an outcome. Do not judge the list. Just notice how much of your week is shaped by it, and set beside it how much is shaped by the one this ayah names. The comparison is the whole exercise.

studies.title: The Cry And The Forgetting
studies.meaning: A sequence rather than a rule. Every blessing is traced to one source; then harm arrives and people call out to that source with a word that means bellowing, not praying; then the harm lifts and a portion of them attach partners to their Lord again. The commentators note the careful limiting word, a portion, which keeps the description from becoming a charge against everyone. The closing line is left ominously short.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just stated that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God and asked why anyone would fear another. This passage answers by describing behaviour rather than argument. Mecca depended on trade routes that ran through drought, raiding and storm at sea, so the experience being described was common: vows made in danger and quietly dropped on arrival. No specific occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: The verb is used of cattle lowing and of a wounded animal's noise. It is not the word for a composed prayer; it names the sound made when composure is gone.

A verb of removing a covering rather than of curing. The harm is treated as something laid over a person and taken off, which makes relief an act performed on them rather than a change in the situation.
An imperative that is not a permission. The same root runs through the Quran for temporary provision, and here the command is a way of leaving people to a course whose end the next clause withholds.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sea travel to Abyssinia and the Yemen was the most frightening thing most Meccans did. Ships were small, crews prayed aloud in storms, and men made vows at the rail that they told stories about afterwards. On land the equivalent was a caravan caught without water. Everyone in the audience had heard someone swear an oath in fear and had watched, weeks later, as it quietly went unmentioned.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for the cry in distress appears only a handful of times in the Quran and always in this setting, of people calling out under pressure. It belongs to animal sound rather than to speech. Choosing it means the passage is not describing insincere prayer; it is describing prayer that is entirely sincere and entirely temporary.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes a claim about human nature that is unusually generous and unusually severe at once. Generous, because it grants that the cry in distress was real and directed rightly, which means the knowledge of God is already there. Severe, because it shows how quickly relief erases it. What is exposed is not disbelief but a memory that works only under pressure, and that is a harder thing to correct.

crossReferences.why: The same pattern at sea: sincere calling in the storm, association again on dry land.
Extends the scene, adding the promises made during the storm and broken after it.
Describes a man calling on his Lord in affliction and forgetting what he called for.

studies.applyIt: Think back to the last time you were genuinely frightened and prayed. Try to recall what you promised, in words or half-words. Most people cannot. Write down one thing you would want to have promised, and do it this week, now that nothing is wrong. The passage is not really about the cry. It is about the fortnight afterwards.

studies.title: A Share For What They Do Not Know
studies.meaning: A practice is described rather than argued with. A portion of harvest and livestock was set aside for objects of worship, and the passage attacks the custom at one precise point. What receives the share is called something they do not know, and what is handed over was provided by God in the first place. The oath that follows attaches the coming questioning not to the giving but to the inventing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Arabian tribes divided produce between God and their deities by a customary allotment, and the surah returns to that practice more than once. The commentators describe the arrangement in general terms and differ over the details of how the shares were separated and what happened when one encroached on the other. The ayah addresses a custom its first hearers already knew rather than a single incident.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary commercial word for a part of something divided among claimants. Using it keeps the practice in the register of accounting, which is exactly where the objection is aimed.
The verb names the giver of the produce before the share is mentioned at all. The grammar leaves nothing that belonged to the allocators, which compresses the whole argument into one word.
A verb for cutting or fashioning something new, used of lies. It presents the deities not as mistaken beliefs quietly inherited but as things actively manufactured by the people now offering to them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Farming and herding communities divided every yield. A portion for the household, a portion for guests and dependants, a portion set aside at a shrine. The allocation happened at the threshing floor or at the pen, in front of witnesses, and within a clan it was effectively a public record. Diverting a share was something the neighbours could see and would remember.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb rendered as they allocate opens three ayat in this surah, each naming a different thing people assign away, and the three sit within seven ayat of one another. Those are its only occurrences in the surah. The repetition builds a short catalogue of misallocation held together by a single word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Generosity towards what does not exist is treated as a theft of attribution rather than a waste of goods. The passage never says the produce was needed elsewhere. It says the produce was never the giver's to assign, which makes the error one of accounting about origins. And because the coming questioning is attached to the invention, what a person answers for is the claim rather than the ritual built on it.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same division of crops and cattle in detail, including how the two shares were handled.
Presses the same point by noting that what they call upon provides them with nothing at all.
Asks who authorised the categories people invent about the provision given to them.

studies.applyIt: Look at where your money actually went last month and pick out one line you would struggle to explain as anything but habit. Not necessarily a wasteful line. Just an unexamined one. The objection in this ayah is to allocation on autopilot, towards something whose claim on you has never once been checked.

studies.title: News Of A Daughter
studies.meaning: Two claims are set side by side and the contradiction between them is left to do the work. Daughters are assigned to God; the speakers keep for themselves what they actually want. Then the passage follows one of those men home and describes his face at the news of a girl. The commentators note that the second ayah does not argue at all. It reports a physical reaction, and the reaction is the refutation.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Some Arabian tribes described certain worshipped figures as daughters of God while placing low value on daughters of their own, and the surah exposes that pairing more than once. The classical commentators describe the attitude towards female children as varying between tribes and households rather than universal, and the Quran addresses it as a practice serious enough to be named directly.

keyTerms.note: The verb normally announces something welcome, and it comes from the word for skin, because good news shows in the face. Followed here by a darkening face, the word is turned against the man.
A form describing a colour deepening as it happens rather than a fixed state. The choice makes the change something the hearer watches, so the news is seen landing on him.
From a root for closing a waterskin tight. It describes swallowing an emotion rather than voicing it, so the man is full of something he has decided not to say aloud.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A birth was announced publicly, and a man received the news in company. Sons meant fighters, herders and heirs who kept property inside the line; daughters married outward and carried a settlement with them into another clan. The economics were real, and an honour system made a family's women a permanent exposure for its reputation. The announcement happened where everyone could watch the father's face.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for the announcement here is the same one the Quran uses elsewhere for the good news brought to Abraham about a son and to Mary about a son. The vocabulary does not change when the child is a girl, and neither does the word for the news itself. Only the man's face changes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage exposes a theology through behaviour rather than through logic. If daughters are attributed to God as a way of assigning Him something lesser, the assigner has already said what he thinks of God. Beyond the specific practice, this establishes a method that runs through the surah: what people do with what they claim to honour is treated as evidence about belief, and admitted as evidence.

crossReferences.why: Puts the buried girl herself in the courtroom, asked for what offence she was killed.
Repeats this darkening face almost word for word, inside the same argument about attribution.
Names daughters first when describing what God grants, reversing the order this passage assumes.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you say you value, then check one recent decision against it. Not a large decision. This passage works by setting a stated belief beside a face at a doorway, and the gap between them is the whole point. Give yourself the same test once, in private, and do not argue with the result.

studies.title: Keep It Or Bury It
studies.meaning: The scene continues and narrows: a man avoiding people, then the two options he turns over. The passage puts both in his own head and neither is good, since keeping the child means keeping her in humiliation and the alternative is covering her in earth. The commentators read the phrasing as a deliberate refusal to offer him a third possibility, because his own premise has already removed it. The closing verdict lands on the reasoning.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The burial of infant girls is reported in the classical sources as the practice of some Arabian groups, driven by poverty and by fear of dishonour, and it is not described as universal. The Quran raises it several times in the Meccan period. The commentators treat this passage as describing the mentality that made the act thinkable rather than reporting one case.

keyTerms.note: A verb for going behind something out of sight. It puts shame before any decision, so the passage shows him managing what others can see before he has considered the child at all.
From a root for lightness and low worth. The word names what he would be keeping her in, which means the option he calls keeping her is already a form of harm.
A verb for thrusting something down out of view, used of concealing rather than of any burial rite. The word does to the child in language what the act does in fact.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Honour in that society was collective and fragile, and a family carried its reputation into every negotiation over trade, marriage and protection. A daughter's future conduct, or her capture in a raid, could be spoken of for a generation. Poverty sharpened all of it. Refusing the practice meant absorbing a cost that a man's whole clan, and not only he, would pay.
studies.didYouKnow: The pronoun the passage attaches to the child in both options is masculine in form, agreeing grammatically with the word for the news rather than with the girl. Classical grammarians discussed the choice at length, and several read it as holding the reader's attention on how the father is thinking rather than on the child herself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verdict at the end falls on the judging, not on the man's grief or his poverty. That distinction matters. It treats the evaluation of a human life as something that can be simply wrong, the way an arithmetic answer is wrong, rather than as one custom to be weighed against other customs. It also establishes that a child's worth is not derived from what she will eventually contribute.

crossReferences.why: Supplies the news and the darkened face that this ayah continues without any break in the sentence.
Returns to the buried girl on the Day of Judgement, and gives her a question of her own.
Names the killing of children out of fear of poverty, and answers that fear directly.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone whose value in your mind is quietly attached to what they provide. A colleague, a relative, a person you find hard work. Say one thing to them this week that has nothing to do with their usefulness to you. The charge in this ayah is against a way of counting, and that is where it can be answered.

studies.title: The Highest Description
studies.meaning: A short ayah with a comparison folded inside it. What is set out is not a moral contrast between two groups but a contrast of descriptions: people who do not expect an afterlife are said to have the description of evil, and God has the loftiest one. The commentators note that the word covers a likeness, a proverb and a set of attributes at once. Two closing names, might and wisdom, say what the loftiest description contains.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the passage about attributing daughters and following it with a general principle. The surah has been showing what people say about God and what they quietly keep for themselves. This ayah names the deeper error, which is that a description of God had been produced at all, assembled out of human preference. No occasion is reported for it in the classical sources.

keyTerms.note: The word covers a comparison, a proverb and a set of attributes. Its width is useful here, because the passage concerns both the pictures people make of God and the ones they make of themselves.
A superlative from a root for elevation. Set against the description of evil rather than against a merely lower one, it puts the two on a single scale with nothing standing between them.
From a root for being rare, strong and out of reach. It names power that cannot be diminished, which is the quality a description assembled out of human wishes would never think to include.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian society ran on likenesses. A poet could fix a tribe's reputation with a single comparison, and a proverb repeated at a gathering settled arguments or ruined families. Descriptions were the currency of honour, memorised and carried between towns by travellers who had heard them once. Claiming the highest description in that setting was a claim made inside a real and competitive economy of speech.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah is unusually dense in comparisons. After this ayah it builds three extended ones, each introduced by the same phrase: a slave who owns nothing set against a man who spends freely, a mute man who is a burden set against one who commands justice, and a secure town that turned ungrateful. The highest likeness is announced first, and the human ones follow.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah moves the argument from what people worship to how they describe, which is a subtler charge. A description assembled to be comforting, or to justify what its maker already wanted, will in the end be a description of the maker. Attaching might and wisdom to the loftiest description then rules out two familiar substitutes at once: a God who can be managed, and a God who is merely arbitrary.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase for the highest description, inside an argument from creation to re-creation.
States the denial that makes this comparison work, that nothing whatever is like Him.
Warns against striking likenesses for God, applying immediately the principle set out here.

studies.applyIt: Write down in one sentence what you assume God is like when you are not thinking about it carefully. The version running underneath your reactions. Then read it back and ask which part came from a verse and which part came from your own hopes or fears. Do not correct it yet. Seeing it clearly is enough for one day.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Postponed To An Appointed Term
studies.meaning: A conditional opens on a deliberately excessive scale: if wrongdoing were answered at once, nothing that moves would be left alive. The commentators note that the sentence takes in animals, so the consequence described would not be confined to the wrongdoers. Then it turns to what actually happens, which is deferral. The last clause shuts the other direction too, because when the appointed term arrives it cannot be shifted by an hour either way.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just described people assigning to God what they themselves dislike, and this ayah answers an objection nobody has spoken aloud: if all this is true, why is nothing happening. The classical commentators treat it as a general statement about how the world is governed rather than a response to a named incident, and report no particular occasion.

keyTerms.note: A reciprocal form of the verb to take, used for calling in what is owed. It belongs to the language of debt and contract, so the sentence describes a claim being enforced rather than anger being expressed.
A fixed period with a known end, used in that society for the due date on a loan. The word holds both the span and the deadline, so the delay described is already measured out.
The smallest unit the sentence could have chosen. Naming it makes the fixity precise in both directions, since the verbs that follow deny delaying the term and bringing it forward alike.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Credit ran the caravan economy. Goods went north against a promise, and a term was set for repayment, witnessed and remembered. Everyone knew what a due date was and what asking for an extension cost a man in standing. A creditor who did not call in a debt immediately was understood to be showing forbearance rather than forgetting. The vocabulary of this ayah belongs to that world.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a creature that moves, used here for what would be wiped out, occurs twice in this surah and only twice. The other occurrence, a dozen ayat earlier, names everything in the heavens and the earth that bows to God. The same term marks the whole of animate creation once as worshipping and once as at risk.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are established together and they pull against each other. Delay is real, so the absence of visible consequence proves nothing about whether wrongdoing registers. And the term is fixed, so the delay is not open-ended and not a negotiation anyone can enter. Between them, the ayah removes both the comfort of thinking nothing is counted and the panic of thinking anything might land at any moment.

crossReferences.why: States the same conditional almost word for word, then names the term and describes its arrival.
Applies the fixed term to whole communities, with the same denial that it can be moved.
Explains the deferral as mercy, supplying the reason this ayah leaves unstated.

studies.applyIt: Think of a consequence you have quietly decided is not coming, because enough time has gone by. A conversation you owe, a debt, a habit. You do not need to panic about it. Just move it back from the settled column into the open one this week, and take the first small step you have been putting off.

studies.title: What Their Tongues Describe
studies.meaning: The last and sharpest of the surah's three allocations. Something is assigned to God that the assigners themselves would not want, and in the same breath their tongues claim the best outcome for themselves. The commentators read the two halves as one gesture, the false attribution and the self-flattery being a single act seen from either end. The response follows without argument, and the phrasing marks it as beyond dispute.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, ending a run of three ayat that each open by describing what people allocate. The surah has moved from a share of produce, to daughters, to this. The classical commentators connect the passage to the Meccan confidence that whatever came after death, the speakers would be fine. No specific occasion is reported, and the attitude is treated as general among the objectors.

keyTerms.note: The verb for giving an account of something's qualities, used of a witness or of a merchant describing goods. Attaching it to tongues makes the lie a piece of testimony rather than a private opinion.
A feminine superlative, the finest of something the sentence never names. That vagueness is part of the claim, since what is being asserted is a general confidence about how things will turn out.
Scholars differ over the reading. Some take it as being driven forward into the Fire, others as being neglected and forgotten there, and the classical commentaries preserve both without settling it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation was made and unmade by speech. A man's word in the market was his credit, and a merchant who described his goods falsely lost the trade of a whole route. Poets were paid to describe, and their descriptions travelled with the caravans. In a culture where a spoken characterisation carried that kind of force, a tongue describing a lie was doing measurable damage.
studies.didYouKnow: The short phrase that introduces the verdict here, a construction meaning without doubt or no escaping it, occurs five times in the Quran, and three of those five are in this surah. It appears once earlier about God knowing what people conceal, once here, and once again near the surah's end.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Self-assessment is treated as a theological claim rather than a mood. To be confident of the best outcome while attributing to God what you would refuse for yourself is to have decided both ends of the account in your own favour. The passage does not answer by disproving the confidence. It answers by naming who holds the verdict, so what is really at stake is where judgement is located.

crossReferences.why: Opens with the same verb of allocating, beginning the short sequence that this ayah closes.
Records the identical confidence, that things will turn out well, in the mouth of a similar speaker.
Dramatises the assumption as a story, with a man certain his garden and his standing will hold.

studies.applyIt: Listen this week for the sentence you use to reassure yourself about how things will end. Most people have one and say it often. Write it down word for word. You do not have to reject it. Just notice that you are the one who said it, and that saying it is not the same as knowing it.

studies.title: Made Alluring To Them
studies.meaning: An oath opens the first ayah, and what follows is a pattern rather than an accusation. Messengers were sent to earlier communities, and something made their own conduct look attractive to them. The commentators note that nothing was added to those deeds; only the appearance changed. The second ayah then names the book's function against exactly that problem. It is sent to settle what people disagree about, and it arrives as guidance and mercy for those who accept it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was meeting rejection that repeated what earlier messengers had met, and the surah keeps placing the present opposition inside that longer series. The classical commentators read the pairing here as consolation and instruction at once. No particular occasion is reported, and the two ayat belong to the surah's argument about how communities receive a message.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for decorating a surface. It leaves the thing itself untouched and alters only how it looks, which is why commentators describe this as a failure of judgement rather than of information.

The word for a protector who holds authority and gives support in return for loyalty. Applying it here inverts a relationship the audience valued, since patronage was the very thing that made life safe.

A reciprocal verb suggesting people pulling in opposite directions rather than holding calm opinions. It names disagreement as a condition the scripture arrives into, not one that the scripture creates.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Patronage held Arabian society together. A man without a protector could be killed on the road with no consequence, so alliances were formal, publicly declared, and worth more than property. Freed slaves and newcomers to a town needed one in order to trade at all. Naming a patron for a whole community was, in that setting, naming who would answer for them when something went wrong.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb rendered as clarify is used twice within these few ayat with the same person as its subject. Earlier the Reminder is sent down so that the messenger may clarify to people what was revealed to them, and here the scripture is sent down so that he may clarify what they dispute. The task is stated twice, with only the second half changed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the difficulty of belief in perception rather than in evidence. If deeds can be made to look good to the person doing them, further argument does not automatically help, which is why the answer given is a book that adjudicates rather than another proof. Guidance and mercy are then named together at the end, so being shown where you are wrong is presented as a kindness.

crossReferences.why: Says that every community has had its own conduct made to look good in its own eyes.
Describes scripture given to a people who then disputed only after clear knowledge reached them.
Sets out the same purpose for revelation, sent to judge between people over what they differed about.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you do that you have never seriously questioned, because it has always looked obviously fine. Ask someone you trust what they see in it. The warning in this ayah is not about doing wrong knowingly. It is about the way a habit stops looking like a choice, and a person outside your head can usually still see it.

studies.title: Revived After Its Death
studies.meaning: One sentence, one image, and then a closing clause that names its audience. Water comes down and dead ground becomes living ground. The commentators read this as the Quran's standard argument for resurrection, offered not as proof but as an annual demonstration nobody disputes. What is unusual is the final word, which specifies people who listen rather than people who think, so the sign is filed under hearing rather than reasoning.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, opening a run of ayat that move from rain to cattle to fruit to bees, each closing on a different kind of person. The surah is answering an audience that accepted God as creator while denying that He would raise the dead. The classical commentators treat the sequence as cumulative rather than as a set of separate occasions, and report no specific event behind it.

keyTerms.note: A causative of the verb to live. It is the same verb used across the Quran for raising the dead, so a sentence about a field is already carrying the vocabulary of the argument it serves.
Land is given an actual death rather than dormancy. The choice of word makes the yearly recovery an instance of the thing being denied rather than a comparison drawn loosely.
The verb for hearing, used here of taking something in and letting it register. It implies a sign that works on a person willing to attend, not one who must first be argued into position.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rain in Arabia was rare, local and dramatic. A valley could stay dry for years and then flood in a night, and within days ground that had been bare would carry grazing. Tribes moved herds towards reported rainfall, and news of it travelled fast between camps. Everyone in the audience had watched a landscape come back, and had staked a season on it happening.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact closing phrase used here, naming a single sign for a people who do something, occurs six times in the Quran, and five of those six are in this surah. Each time the last word changes: those who reflect, who remember, who listen, who understand, and who reflect again.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument treats resurrection as a question about power that has already been answered in public. If reviving what is dead were impossible, it would not be happening every spring in front of the people objecting. What the passage adds is that the sign is available to whoever will listen, which places the obstacle in attention rather than in intelligence or in access to evidence.

crossReferences.why: Draws the conclusion this ayah leaves implicit, naming the reviver of the earth as the reviver of the dead.
Uses the stirring of dry ground as a direct answer to a question about being raised.
Sends winds driving cloud to dead land, and calls the resurrection just such an emergence.

studies.applyIt: The next time it rains where you are, go to a window and stay there for one minute without doing anything else. That is the whole exercise. The closing word of this ayah is about listening, and rain is one of the few signs that arrives with a sound. Let it be a sign once instead of weather.

studies.title: From Between Waste And Blood
studies.meaning: The passage announces a lesson and then shows its working, which is unusual. It traces milk backwards to where it comes from, and it does not soften the description. Something clean and pleasant emerges from a place that is neither. The commentators read the point as separation rather than transformation: what is produced is kept distinct from its surroundings, and the word for pure is carrying that argument.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, inside the sequence of signs drawn from ordinary life. Herd animals were the wealth of the audience, and milk was a daily staple rather than a luxury. The classical commentators note that this ayah and one elsewhere in the Quran open with identical wording before diverging. No specific occasion is reported, and the surah is reasoning from what its hearers handled every morning.

keyTerms.note: From a root for passing from one bank of a river to the other. The word names a thought that carries you from what you see to what it implies, which is what the rest of the ayah then performs.
A word for something separated out and left free of any admixture. Placed immediately after the two things named beside it, it insists on distinctness rather than on cleanliness.
From a root for going down the throat without resistance. It adds the drinker's own experience to the description, so the sign includes how the thing feels and not only what it is.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A herd was a family's bank. Camels and goats were counted as wealth, given as bride price, paid as compensation, and milked twice daily for the household. Milk was drunk fresh, soured for keeping, and thinned with water on journeys when nothing else could be carried. A poor season showed first in the milk, so anyone could read an animal's condition at a glance.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and one in a later surah begin with word-for-word the same clause about cattle and a lesson, then go different ways. The pronoun attached to the animals' bellies differs between the two, masculine here and feminine there, and classical grammarians wrote at length about which noun each of them agrees with.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The example is chosen so that the process, and not only the product, carries the argument. Anyone can be grateful for milk. This ayah insists on where it comes from, which makes divine provision something that works through ordinary biology rather than around it. It also sets a pattern the surah repeats: what is valuable is often produced quietly inside something an observer would rather not examine.

crossReferences.why: Opens with identical wording about cattle and a lesson, then turns to their other uses instead.
Introduces the same animals earlier in this surah, listing warmth and food among their benefits.
Returns to livestock as something people did not make, and asks why gratitude does not follow.

studies.applyIt: Drink something slowly today and notice the moment it goes down easily. That specific quality is named in this ayah, and it is there because the sign is meant to include the drinking and not only the milk. Most gratitude fails at the point where a thing is too ordinary to register. This is one attempt at catching it before it slips.

studies.title: Inspired To The Bee
studies.meaning: Fruit is named first, and the passage observes without comment that people take two different things from it, one intoxicating and one wholesome food. The commentators read the pairing as a contrast drawn deliberately and left unresolved at this stage. Then the direction changes completely and an instruction is given to an insect, in the feminine singular, telling it where to build. What is described is guidance reaching a creature with no language.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah takes its name from this passage. The classical commentators note that the ayah about grapes and dates came before the later Medinan passages that address intoxicants, which is why it can describe the practice plainly. Beyond that they report no particular occasion. The section belongs to the surah's run of signs drawn from familiar agriculture and familiar animals.

keyTerms.note: Named beside wholesome provision with no verdict attached. The commentators note the plain contrast between the two words, and read the ayah as describing what people do rather than evaluating it.

The verb ordinarily used for revelation given to prophets. Applied to an insect, it names an instruction arriving without language, which is why commentators call it a different mode of the same thing.
A feminine singular imperative, addressed to the bee the way one addresses a person. The grammar makes the instruction direct rather than general, and the bee is the one being spoken to.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wild honey was gathered from cliffs and hollow trees, and it was valuable enough to trade and to give as a gift. Date palms and vines were the two great cultivated crops of the oases, and both were pressed. A household's year ran on the date harvest, which was counted, stored and borrowed against. Bees, palms and vines were the ordinary furniture of an oasis economy.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the bee occurs exactly once in the whole Quran, in this passage, and the surah is named after it even though it runs to a hundred and twenty-eight ayat on many other subjects. The same verb of inspiration is used elsewhere of the mother of Moses and of the heavens themselves.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Using the vocabulary of revelation for an insect does something careful. It says guidance is a category wider than prophecy, and that the world is full of creatures being told what to do in ways they never experience as instruction. That makes prophecy the human form of something general rather than an exception in an otherwise silent universe, and it makes the bee's competence evidence rather than charm.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb of inspiration for the mother of Moses, outside the line of prophets.
Applies the same verb to the heavens, extending it to something further still from speech.
Returns to these two products of the vine and weighs their benefit against their harm.

studies.applyIt: Watch a bee or an ant for one minute this week without interrupting it. You will see competence nobody taught it and it cannot explain. The claim in this passage is that the competence is instruction, arriving in a form the creature never recognises as instruction. Sit with that for the length of one small animal's errand.

studies.title: The Pathways Of Your Lord
studies.meaning: The instruction to the bee continues: eat from every fruit, then travel your Lord's paths, and a single word describes the manner. Scholars differ over whether it describes the paths as smoothed or the bee as compliant, and both readings are old. What follows is stated as fact rather than promise. A drink of varied colours emerges, and in it is healing for people, which the sentence leaves unqualified.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, completing the passage that gives the surah its name. Honey was a known remedy in Arabia long before this ayah, used on wounds and for stomach complaints, so the statement would not have startled the first hearers. The classical commentators report no specific occasion. They read the closing phrase about reflection as marking the end of the whole run of signs.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a road or track. Attaching it to the Lord makes the bee's foraging routes something assigned rather than chosen, and it is the same word the Quran uses for the ways of guidance.
Scholars differ over what this modifies. Some read the paths as smoothed for the bee, others the bee as compliant along them, and both readings are preserved in the classical commentaries.
An indefinite noun, so the sentence says healing rather than the healing. Commentators generally read it as real but partial, describing a genuine remedy rather than a cure for everything.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medicine in seventh-century Arabia was made of what could be carried: dates, oil, herbs, cupping, cautery and honey. Honey kept without spoiling on long journeys, which mattered enormously, and it was put on wounds as well as swallowed. Physicians were rare and households treated themselves. Naming honey as a healing named something already in most tents rather than introducing a new remedy.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for healing occurs four times in the Quran. Three of those describe revelation itself, healing what is in the chests or given to those who believe. This is the only place where the Quran applies the word to a physical substance, and the substance comes out of an insect.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts the bee's obedience and the honey's usefulness inside one sentence, so following an assigned path and producing something that helps others are presented as a single movement rather than two. It also refuses to make the healing a reward for anything. It simply emerges, from the bellies of insects doing as they were told, which places the benefit downstream of an obedience nobody involved understands.

crossReferences.why: Calls revelation a healing, using the very word this ayah applies to honey.
Names a healing for what is in the chests, giving the same word its inward sense.
Carries the instruction that this ayah completes, telling the bee where to build its houses.

studies.applyIt: Think of the smallest useful thing you do that nobody notices, and do it once more this week without mentioning it. The bee here is not praised, thanked, or told what its work becomes. It eats, it travels its route, and something people need comes out of that. Try that shape for one task.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Back To The Frailest Age
studies.meaning: Three movements are compressed into one sentence: created, taken, and for some a return to an age the ayah calls the meanest. The final clause is precise about what is lost, which is knowledge already acquired rather than knowledge never had. The commentators note that this is not presented as punishment. It sits among signs, and the two names at the close, knowing and capable, are the frame the passage offers for holding it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, among the ayat that take their signs from the human life span rather than from crops and animals. The surah has just described milk, fruit and honey, and here it turns the same attention on the body that consumes them. The classical commentators report no particular occasion, and read the ayah as a general statement about the course a human life can take.

keyTerms.note: A verb from the language of settling accounts, meaning to receive in full what is owed. Death is described as a completed collection rather than as a loss, which is a deliberate choice of register.
A superlative for what is lowest in value or condition. The word is blunt, and commentators observe that the Quran does not soften its description of extreme old age at this point.
The whole allotted stretch of a life rather than a moment within it. Pairing it with the previous word makes the phrase name a stage inside a span, not an accident that befalls someone.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Age was authority. Elders settled disputes, held genealogies, and carried the poetry and treaty terms that nobody had written down. A community's memory lived inside its oldest members. So the loss described here was not a private matter: when an elder stopped knowing, a tribe lost records it had no other copy of, and everyone understood exactly what that cost.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase for this stage of life appears twice in the Quran and nowhere else. The other occurrence sits inside a long argument for resurrection that runs from a drop of fluid through birth and growth to old age, and then to dry ground stirring under rain. Both uses stand in passages about what God is able to do.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah places the undoing of a person inside the ordinary providence it has been describing, which is uncomfortable and deliberate. Knowing and capable are named at exactly the point where a human being is neither. That makes the two attributes a statement about who holds the account when the person can no longer hold it, and it locates dignity somewhere other than in capacity.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical phrase for this stage, inside a longer argument about being raised again.
Traces the same arc, weakness to strength to weakness and grey hair, as a created pattern.
Says whoever is granted long life is reversed in creation, and asks whether people consider it.

studies.applyIt: Sit with someone old this week, particularly someone whose memory has begun to go. Do not test them and do not correct their dates. Just be there for the length of one cup of tea. This ayah names knowing and capable at the exact moment a person is neither, and that is easier to believe in company than alone.

studies.title: They Would Not Level It
studies.meaning: An observation about unequal provision is followed by an argument that turns the hearers' own conduct into its premise. Those given more do not hand their property to the people they own until both stand level. The commentators read this as exposing an inconsistency: the same people who guarded every degree of their own advantage were assigning partners to God in what He owns. The closing question then names the whole thing as denial.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Bonded service was an ordinary feature of the society addressed, and the ayah takes the arrangement as its audience knew it in order to reason from it. The classical commentators note that the passage is not describing what ought to happen with property but reasoning from what visibly does happen. No specific occasion is reported for it in the sources.

keyTerms.note: A verb for granting a surplus over another. It states the inequality as something given rather than earned, which removes the ground on which the favoured party might otherwise feel entitled.
The word for two things standing at exactly the same height. Its appearance is the hinge of the argument, because levelling is precisely what the property holders would never grant.
A verb for rejecting what you actually recognise. It differs from simple disbelief, so the charge is not ignorance of the favour but refusal to acknowledge something already known.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Households in Mecca included people who were owned, and the line between them and the free ran through every detail of daily life: where you sat, what you were called, whether your word counted in a dispute. Property was the clearest marker of all, and a man who blurred it lost standing among his peers. Everyone listening knew exactly how firm that line was.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb that closes this ayah is not the usual Quranic word for disbelief. It names a denial made against one's own recognition, and the Quran uses it elsewhere of people who rejected signs while, in its words, their own selves were certain of them. Choosing it here turns ingratitude into a claim about what a person actually knows.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument works by making the hearers apply their own standard to themselves. If you would not share ownership with someone in your household, you have already shown that you understand what exclusive possession means, so attributing partners to God is not a position you hold consistently. Ingratitude is then redefined. It is not a failure to feel thankful but a refusal to draw an obvious conclusion.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same argument in almost the same terms, drawn from partners in what people already own.
Uses the same verb for denial, and adds that their own selves were certain of what they rejected.
Returns to the distribution of livelihood and says the ranking between people is itself assigned.

studies.applyIt: Notice one advantage you have that you did not arrange: where you were born, a language you speak, a body that works. Then notice how quickly you defend it as yours. You do not need to give it away. Just say once, in plain words to yourself, that it was handed to you, and let the sentence sit there.

studies.title: Children And Grandchildren
studies.meaning: A list of gifts arrives in a single breath, and its order matters. Partners drawn from among the hearers themselves, then children from those partners, then a further generation, then good things to eat. It moves outward through a household and forward through time. The commentators differ over the exact reference of one word in the list. Then the sentence turns and asks how people fed by all this can trust what is empty.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been listing what people receive and then asking what they do with it, and here the list becomes domestic. The classical commentators differ over whether one term names grandchildren, servants or relatives by marriage, and they preserve the range without settling it. No specific occasion is reported. The audience addressed counted lineage as the central form of wealth.

keyTerms.note: A word for one of a matched pair, used of both sexes. Saying they come from among yourselves stresses shared kind rather than difference, and that is where the sentence begins its argument.
The word occurs only here in the Quran. Commentators read it as grandchildren, as servants, or as those who assist, and all three senses come from a root for swift, willing service.
A plural covering what is pleasant and clean, most often of food. It closes the list by moving from people to provision, so the household and its table are named together as one gift.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man's standing was counted in descendants. Sons and their sons meant defence, labour, and a name that outlived him, while a line that ended was spoken of with pity. Marriages were negotiated between clans and sealed alliances that outlasted the couple. A second generation of children was visible proof that a household had held together, which in that world was an achievement worth naming aloud.
studies.didYouKnow: One word in this ayah, usually translated as grandchildren, occurs nowhere else in the Quran. Its root has to do with speed and eager service, which is why some classical commentators read it as helpers rather than descendants. The lexicons record both senses side by side without resolving which the ayah intends.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats family as provision, and that is a specific claim. Spouses, children and a further generation are placed in the same list as food, all of them given rather than achieved. It undercuts the reading of lineage as an accomplishment, which was the going assumption of the audience. The closing contrast then sets falsehood against favour, so misplaced trust and ingratitude are named as one movement.

crossReferences.why: Describes partners made from among yourselves, and names affection and mercy as the sign in it.
Continues the theme of children as something granted, with the choice explicitly not the parents'.
Places wealth and sons together as the adornment of this life, and weighs them against what lasts.

studies.applyIt: Say one specific thank you to a family member this week for something they have simply always done. Not a general appreciation. Name the thing. This ayah lists people alongside food as provision, and the point of that ordering is that the nearest gifts are the first ones to stop registering.

studies.title: God Knows And You Do Not
studies.meaning: The first ayah describes what is served besides God by a double negative: it owns no provision, from sky or earth, and has no capacity to acquire any. The second draws the instruction out. Do not coin likenesses for God, and the reason given is a bare contrast between His knowing and the hearers' not knowing. The commentators note that the prohibition falls on the activity of comparing rather than on one particular comparison.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, arriving straight after the surah has inventoried what people actually receive: rain, milk, honey, spouses, children. The instruction follows from that inventory, since the objects being served had contributed nothing to it. The classical commentators report no specific occasion, and read the pair as the hinge into the extended comparisons that occupy the next several ayat.

keyTerms.note: The verb for holding legal possession, which in that society implied the ability to give away. Denying it says the thing served cannot transfer anything, for the simple reason that it holds nothing.

Literally to strike, used both of minting coins and of framing a comparison. The idiom treats a likeness as something manufactured, which suits an argument about people fashioning descriptions of God.
A plural with the definite article, so the prohibition covers the practice rather than a single instance. The same word returns immediately afterwards with God as the one doing the striking.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Comparison was the standard tool of Arabic thought. Genealogy, poetry and the settling of disputes all worked by likening one case to another, and a man who produced the right comparison in an assembly won the argument outright. Telling that audience to stop coining likenesses in one particular area was telling skilled practitioners to set down the instrument they trusted most.
studies.didYouKnow: The prohibition here is followed immediately by three likenesses that God strikes in the ayat just after, each introduced by the very verb the hearers have been told not to use. The surah forbids the activity and then performs it within two lines, which classical commentators read as a statement about who is qualified to do it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reason attached to the prohibition is unusual. It is not that comparison is disrespectful but that the people doing it lack the information. A likeness works by drawing on what you already know, so any comparison a person invents for God will be assembled out of what that person happens to have met. The prohibition therefore concerns method, and the ayat that follow demonstrate the method done properly.

crossReferences.why: Begins the comparisons God strikes, immediately after the hearers are told not to strike their own.
Supplies the principle behind the prohibition, that nothing whatever resembles Him.
Sets out a likeness about what is served besides God, which cannot create even a fly.

studies.applyIt: Catch yourself the next time you explain God with a comparison, especially one that begins with a person. A parent, a judge, a friend. You do not have to abandon it. Just add a sentence afterwards naming where the comparison breaks down, and notice how much of your picture was resting on the part that broke.

studies.title: Are They Equal In Comparison
studies.meaning: The first of the likenesses arrives, built entirely out of the audience's own social world.
