A bonded man with power over nothing is set beside someone given generous provision who spends from it privately and openly. The question that follows is never answered directly. The commentators note that the praise interrupting the comparison stands in place of the answer, and the closing clause says most people do not know this.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just forbidden people to coin their own likenesses, and this is the first that God strikes in reply. The comparison uses bonded servitude as an available fact of the society rather than as an endorsement of it. The classical commentators report no particular occasion, and read the two figures as standing for what is served besides God and for God Himself.

keyTerms.note: A passive participle from the verb to own, so the man is defined entirely by another's possession of him. The word leaves him with no capacity of his own that the sentence could describe.
From a root for a thing passing out and away. The verb covers all giving out of what one holds, and the surrounding words make the giving continuous rather than occasional.
Paired here with openly, so both are approved together. The two describe giving that is not managed for an audience, since someone doing both is not calculating who happens to be watching.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Bonded servitude was visible everywhere in Mecca, and the powerlessness described here was legal rather than figurative. A bonded man could not own, could not give, could not enter a contract. Against him the audience would have pictured a merchant of standing whose generosity was known in the market and also, by reputation, practised where nobody saw it. Both figures were people they could name.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the first of three comparisons in this surah introduced by the identical phrase about God striking a likeness. The other two follow within forty ayat, one about a man who cannot speak and one about a town that had been secure. Together they form the surah's longest sustained sequence of parables.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The comparison turns on capacity to give, which is a precise way to argue about what deserves worship. What is served besides God is not called evil but unable, and inability is the disqualification. Placing praise in the middle of the question does something too: the right response is supplied before the reader has finished working the comparison out, as though the answer were never in doubt.

crossReferences.why: Forbids the hearers to strike likenesses immediately before this one is struck for them.
Commends spending by night and day, secretly and openly, in the same paired phrasing.
Says that what is called upon besides God does not own the skin of a date stone.

studies.applyIt: Give something away this week that nobody will find out about. It does not need to be money and it does not need to be large. The comparison here praises giving done openly and unseen together, and the unseen half is the part that tells you whether the open half was really about giving at all.

studies.title: A Burden On His Guardian
studies.meaning: The second comparison sharpens the first. One man cannot speak, has power over nothing, and is a weight on whoever answers for him; sent anywhere, he brings back nothing good. The other commands justice and is himself on a straight road. The commentators note that the second figure is described twice over, by what he tells others to do and by where he stands, so his speech and his position are made to agree.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, the second of three likenesses struck in reply to hearers who had been coining their own. The classical commentators read the mute figure as standing for what was served besides God, unable to answer or to benefit anyone, and the other as standing for God, or in some readings for the person who calls to Him. No specific occasion is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: A form describing someone without speech from birth rather than someone silent by choice. The related plural is used elsewhere in the Quran of people who possess speech but will not use it for truth.
A word for something that must be carried and returns nothing. It is blunt about dependence, and commentators apply it to the object of worship in the comparison rather than to any human being.
A word covering both the one who owns and the one who protects. Its double sense keeps the figure inside a relationship of care, so the burden is being carried by someone obliged to carry it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A household took responsibility for its dependants absolutely, including those who could not work or speak for themselves. Nobody was turned out; the clan absorbed the cost, and that was a point of honour. The arithmetic was still discussed, though. Sending a man on an errand and having him come back with nothing was a familiar frustration in an economy where every journey cost water and days.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the mute man occurs in this exact singular form only once in the Quran. Its plural is used several times elsewhere, always of people described as deaf, mute and blind while their faculties in fact work. The singular is reserved for a comparison, and the plural for an accusation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: This comparison adds speech to the capacity that the previous one weighed. What cannot answer cannot be in a relationship, so the objection to serving it is not that it is weak but that nothing passes in either direction. Describing the alternative as commanding justice while standing on a straight path also joins two things people habitually separate: telling others what is right, and being where you say they should be.

crossReferences.why: Strikes the first of these comparisons, weighing capacity to give rather than capacity to speak.
Presses the same point, that what is called upon does not answer and possesses no faculties.
Uses the plural of this word for people whose senses work but who bring nothing back.

studies.applyIt: Think of one place where what you tell other people is right and where you actually stand have drifted apart. Do not announce it to anyone. Just close the gap by a single visible step this week, in the direction of the thing you already say. This comparison praises the man who commands justice only alongside where his own feet are.

studies.title: As A Blink Or Nearer
studies.meaning: Two claims are joined by a conjunction doing more work than it appears to. Everything hidden in the heavens and the earth belongs to God, and the arrival of the Hour is a blink of an eye or quicker. The commentators read the second as describing the speed of the command rather than the duration of the event. A third clause closes with power, so hiddenness, speed and capacity are stated as a single thought.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, coming after the comparisons and before the surah turns to the birth of the human being. The audience had repeatedly demanded to know when the Hour would come, and the surah opened by saying the command of God had already drawn near. The classical commentators treat this as part of that running response rather than an answer to a question asked on some particular day.

keyTerms.note: What is absent from perception rather than what is mysterious in itself. Placing it in a possessive relationship with God makes hiddenness relative, since a thing unseen has to be unseen by someone.
The ordinary word for a portion of time, used as a name for the end. Its plainness is deliberate, so the event is referred to by a term for something short rather than something vast.
The flick of the eye, the fastest movement a person could point to. The comparison takes its unit from the body rather than from the sky, which keeps an unimaginable speed measurable.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Time in Arabia was measured by things that took a while: a moon, a season, the days a caravan needed to reach Gaza, the years of a boycott. Fast events were reckoned by the body, a breath or a glance. Choosing the blink as the measure meant reaching for the shortest interval anyone in the audience had a name for, and one they could test on themselves.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase comparing something to the blink of an eye occurs twice in the Quran, here and in a much shorter later surah, and both times it describes the speed of God's command rather than the scale of what the command accomplishes. The two occurrences use slightly different grammar for the identical image.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Joining the unseen to the speed of the Hour answers a specific objection. If people cannot say when the end will come, that is because knowledge of it is held elsewhere, not because it is far away, and the second clause removes distance from the question entirely. What is left is capacity, named at the close, so the passage leaves the reader with the one fact that does not depend on timing.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same image of a blink, applied there to the singleness of God's command.
Opens this surah by saying the command of God has come, so it should not be hastened.
Lists knowledge of the Hour among the things kept with God and with nobody else.

studies.applyIt: Blink once, deliberately, and notice how little time that was. This ayah uses your own eye as its unit of measure, which means the comparison is available to you at any moment and needs no equipment. Reach for it the next time something feels too far off to be worth preparing for.

studies.title: Not Knowing Anything
studies.meaning: Birth is described as arriving with nothing, and the emptiness is stated first so that what follows reads as equipment rather than as nature. Hearing, sight and the inner faculty are given, in that order, and the commentators note the sequence matches how a newborn actually meets the world. The purpose clause at the end does not say so that you may understand. It says so that you may be grateful, which is a different destination for the same instruments.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, part of the surah's long inventory of what people receive. The passage has just described extreme old age and the loss of knowledge already acquired; here it turns to the other end of a life and describes the moment before any knowledge at all. The classical commentators report no particular occasion, and read the ayah as completing the arc the previous one began.

keyTerms.note: Given in the singular while the words beside it are plural. Classical grammarians discussed the difference at length, most reading hearing as one undivided capacity where seeing is many separate acts.
A plural, which commentators connect to the many distinct things a person looks at. Its pairing with a singular word for hearing is among the ayah's most discussed features.
The lexicons connect this root to an animal that yields well on little pasture. Gratitude in that image is a return larger than what came in, rather than a bare acknowledgement of it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Infant mortality was high, and birth was attended by the women of a household without physicians. A child who lived was named on the seventh day and its arrival announced through the clan. Nothing about a newborn was assumed, least of all that it would hear and see. Families watched for the first response to a sound and remembered afterwards when it came.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for hearing in this ayah is singular, while the words for sight and for the inner faculty are both plural. The asymmetry is pronounced enough that classical grammarians wrote about it repeatedly, most explaining that hearing is one undivided capacity while seeing consists of many separate acts, each with its own object.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Putting the purpose clause at gratitude rather than at knowledge changes what the faculties are for. They are not described as tools for working out the truth, though they can be used that way. They are described as gifts whose proper use includes noticing that they were given. That makes ingratitude the misuse of an instrument rather than merely an omission of good manners.

crossReferences.why: Lists the same three faculties as given after the shaping, and closes on how little thanks follows.
Repeats the three and adds the same complaint, that thanks is rarely given for them.
Describes the other end of the same life, when knowledge already acquired is taken away.

studies.applyIt: Pick one of the three named here and use it deliberately for five minutes today. Listen to something without looking at a screen, or look at something without narrating it to yourself. This ayah attaches these faculties to gratitude rather than to knowledge, and gratitude usually needs the equipment noticed before it will work at all.

studies.title: Nothing Holds Them Up
studies.meaning: A question again, and a scene anyone can check. Birds are suspended in open air, and the sentence lets a negative do the work: nothing holds them except God. The commentators note that the word describing their state means made subject rather than free, so the flight is presented as an arrangement instead of an achievement. The closing clause then names signs in the plural, which nothing else in this long sequence does.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, resuming the sequence of signs after the passage of comparisons. Bird flight was something Arabians attended to closely, since birds were read for omens and watched as indicators of water. The classical commentators report no particular occasion for the ayah, and read it as of a piece with the surah's method of pointing at what its audience already looked at every day.

keyTerms.note: A collective noun rather than a plural, so it names birds as a category and not a countable group. The sentence is looking at flight itself rather than at any particular flock overhead.
A passive participle used elsewhere in the Quran of the sun, the moon and the sea. It places birds among things arranged for a purpose rather than among things acting on their own account.
The word occurs only here in the Quran. It names the empty space between ground and sky, so the ayah is precise about where the birds are: in nothing at all.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Birds were read professionally. Diviners took omens from the direction a startled bird flew, and travellers watched for species that meant water within a day's ride. Falconry was known among the wealthy. A society that attentive to birds had never asked what kept them up, because the question does not arise while you are using an animal as an instrument.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only ayah in the surah's long sequence of signs that uses the plural. Five others close with the same phrase about a single sign for a people who reflect, remember, listen or understand. This one alone says signs, and it alone names its audience as people who believe rather than people who think.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah locates the marvel in continuation rather than in origin. It does not ask who made birds. It asks what is holding them at this moment, which turns an argument about creation into an argument about maintenance. That reframing matters, because a world needing to be held at every instant is not a machine that was wound once and left, and the difference is the whole distance between two ideas of God.

crossReferences.why: Asks the same question about birds spreading and folding their wings, and gives the same answer.
Says God holds the sky from falling on the earth, using a related verb of holding.
Describes God holding the heavens and the earth from slipping, extending this to everything.

studies.applyIt: Watch a bird stay up without flapping for as long as it lasts. Gulls and crows do it on any windy afternoon. The ayah asks what is holding it, not what built it, and that is a different question from the one most arguments about God get stuck on. Ask the ayah's version once, outdoors.

studies.title: Homes That Travel With You
studies.meaning: Two kinds of dwelling are named in a single sentence and neither is ranked above the other. Built houses give rest; tents made from hides are light enough to move on the day of departure and raise again on the day of settling. Then the list runs on into wool, camel fur and goat hair. The commentators note that everything named comes from animals the surah introduced earlier, so the inventory closes a circle.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The audience included settled townspeople and families who still moved with their herds, and this ayah addresses both without preferring either way of living. The classical commentators note the precision of its vocabulary, which distinguishes three different animal fibres by name. No specific occasion is reported, and the ayah belongs to the run of favours the surah has been setting out.

keyTerms.note: From the root for stillness. It names what a house is for rather than what it is made of, so the gift being described is the quieting rather than the structure that produces it.
The word occurs only here in the Quran. It is the technical term for a household moving with its herds, and its presence marks the ayah as spoken to people who actually did that.
One of three fibres named separately, alongside sheep wool and goat hair. The distinction belongs to a herder rather than a poet, and this word too occurs nowhere else in the Quran.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A black tent was woven from goat hair, which swells when wet and turns the rain, and it could be struck and loaded in under an hour. Wool went into clothing and bedding, camel fur into rope and coarse cloth. A family's tent was often made by its women over years and repaired panel by panel, so the dwelling was literally the household's own work.
studies.didYouKnow: Two words in this one ayah appear nowhere else in the Quran: the term for a household striking camp, and the word for camel fur. Both belong to the technical vocabulary of herding life, and finding them together in a single sentence is one of the clearest signs of how closely this surah tracks its audience's daily work.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Listing a permanent house and a portable one in the same breath refuses to make settlement the mark of a blessed life. Both are described as given. The closing phrase then attaches a limit to all of it, saying enjoyment for a time, and that qualification does quiet work: the comfort is real and the holding is temporary, and the ayah declines to resolve the tension it has just created.

crossReferences.why: Introduces the same animals earlier in this surah, before their hides and fibres are itemised here.
Describes houses God permitted to be raised, where His name is remembered, adding another sense.
Weighs what is given for enjoyment for a time against what remains with God instead.

studies.applyIt: Look around the room you are in and find one thing that came from an animal or a plant, then trace it back two steps in your head. Wool, cotton, leather, wood. This ayah names its fibres separately because the giver of a thing is easier to see while the thing has not yet become a category.

studies.title: Garments Against Heat And Harm
studies.meaning: Four provisions in one sentence, every one of them about shelter: shade out of what has been created, hollows in the mountains, garments against the heat, and garments against each other's violence. The commentators note the last pairing especially, since a single word covers cloth for the sun and armour for battle. The sentence closes on completion, and then on a purpose, and the purpose named is submission rather than thanks.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the surah's inventory of favours before it turns to those who refuse them. The provisions listed belong to travel and to conflict, the two conditions in which a Meccan felt most exposed. The classical commentators report no specific occasion, and observe that this ayah completes the list the preceding ones had been building.

keyTerms.note: The word occurs only here in the Quran. It names natural cavities in rock used as refuge from sun and storm, so the shelter being described is found rather than built by anyone.
A word for a garment worn over the body. It appears twice in this ayah and once more in the Quran, where it describes garments of pitch worn by the guilty.
A word for force and hardship in war. Saying the garments protect you from your own violence places the danger among the hearers themselves rather than somewhere outside them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Travellers timed their journeys around shade, resting through the worst hours under a rock overhang or a solitary tree. Caves in the hills around Mecca served as shelter and as retreat. Armour was expensive, mostly mail brought from the north, and a coat of it could be the most valuable object a family owned. Every item on this list was survival rather than comfort.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used twice here for a garment appears only once elsewhere in the Quran, and there it describes garments of pitch. The same term covers what protects the body in this life and what covers the guilty in the next, an echo classical commentators noted and read as deliberate rather than accidental.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Ending a list of favours with armour is unexpected. It admits that human violence is a permanent condition to be protected against rather than a problem the passage intends to solve, which is unusually plain. The purpose named at the close is submission rather than gratitude, so a favour completed is presented as an argument: what has been fully provided for has no remaining case for holding back.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for garments, there made of pitch, in a description of the guilty.
Names the making of armour as something taught, to protect people from their own violence.
Uses the same language of a favour completed, there of a way of life brought to perfection.

studies.applyIt: Put on a coat this week and notice, for one second, that it is doing a job. Most protection works by being unremarkable. This ayah lists shade, caves and clothing as favours precisely because they are the things a person stops seeing, and it asks you to complete the list yourself before the weather turns.

studies.title: They Know It Then Deny It
studies.meaning: Three short movements. The messenger's responsibility is limited to delivering plainly, which lifts the outcome off him entirely. Then comes the surah's sharpest diagnosis: they recognise the favour and then deny it, so the problem was never that they missed it. Then the scene jumps forward to a day when a witness is raised from every community and no plea is admitted. The commentators read the three as cause and consequence.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, at the point where the surah turns from its catalogue of favours to the response that catalogue received. The classical commentators connect the first ayah to the distress the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) felt at the rejection he was meeting, though they present it as general consolation rather than tying it to a named event. The passage belongs to the surah's later Meccan argument.

keyTerms.note: A noun for getting a message all the way to its destination. It defines the task by arrival rather than by acceptance, which is exactly where the responsibility is being cut off.
A verb for knowing something by acquaintance, the way one knows a face. It makes the denial that follows a refusal rather than an error, since what is denied has already been identified.
From a root for seeking to remove another's displeasure. The passive denies them not forgiveness but the opportunity to plead for it, which is a narrower and colder refusal.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An envoy between tribes carried words he had not written and was not answerable for how they landed, only for delivering them exactly. His safety rested on that understanding, and harming an envoy was among the gravest offences a group could commit. The audience knew the role precisely, so limiting a messenger's duty to clear delivery drew on a category they already had.
studies.didYouKnow: The line about raising a witness from every community appears twice in this surah, five ayat apart, with one preposition changed and a clause added the second time. The first occurrence leaves the witness unspecified and ends with excuses refused. The second names the addressee himself as a witness against the people before him.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Separating delivery from result protects two things at once. It keeps a messenger from measuring himself by how many accept, and it keeps the audience's refusal from being anyone else's fault. The middle ayah then makes that refusal deliberate rather than uninformed, which is what allows the last one to close off excuses without unfairness. Recognition, once established, is what makes an excuse unavailable.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the raising of a witness from every community, adding the messenger as a witness there.
States the same limit on the messenger's duty, that only conveying is upon him.
Shows communities acknowledging that messengers came, and testifying against themselves.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you keep telling someone who does not want to hear it. Say it once more, plainly and kindly, and then stop keeping score. This passage separates delivering a message from securing a result, and most of the exhaustion in a relationship like that comes from having quietly taken on the second job.

studies.title: Surely You Are Liars
studies.meaning: Two scenes, each opening with the same word for seeing. In the first, those who wronged see the punishment and two things are denied together: reduction and delay. In the second, those who associated partners see those partners and immediately point at them, presenting them almost as evidence. What comes back is one flat sentence calling them liars. The commentators note that the accused do not defend themselves; they reject the account.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been building towards this scene since it described people allocating shares to what they did not know. The classical commentators read the exchange as a general depiction of that day rather than a report about named individuals, and they record no occasion for it. The audience addressed had a working relationship with intermediaries they expected would speak for them.

keyTerms.note: A verb for making a load lighter. Denying it addresses a specific hope, that a sentence once passed might still be negotiated downward, which was ordinary practice in tribal arbitration.
From the root for looking, used idiomatically for allowing someone more time. It closes off the second thing a debtor would ask for, so both usual concessions are refused together.
A commercial word for those who share in a venture. Calling them ours keeps the possessive relationship intact even at this moment, which commentators read as the habit outlasting the belief.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Business in Mecca ran on partnership. Caravans were financed by several investors, profits split by agreed share, and disputes settled by arbitration in which each side named backers to speak for it. The word used here belonged to that world, and so did the situation described: a man discovering in front of an arbiter that his partners will not stand with him.
studies.didYouKnow: The two ayat open with exactly the same three words, changing only the description of who is doing the seeing: those who wronged, then those who associated partners. The parallel construction presents the second sight as continuous with the first, so the punishment and the partners come into view within one movement rather than two.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The exchange establishes something about false attachments: they do not survive the moment they were supposed to be useful. What was served is not shown to be powerless in argument but uninterested, which is a colder result than defeat. And refusing to lighten or to delay makes the day a settlement rather than a negotiation, so whatever a person brings into it is already fixed on arrival.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same question about their partners, and reports the denial that immediately follows.
Has the associates disown their followers, and the call made to them go unanswered.
Continues this scene directly, with submission offered once the partners have gone.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you are relying on that has never actually been tested. A relationship, a reputation, a plan. You do not need to abandon it. Just ask, in one honest sentence, what it would do if you needed it tomorrow, and notice whether you already know the answer.

studies.title: Punishment Above Punishment
studies.meaning: The passage adds a second count to the charge. Submission is offered and the inventions desert their makers, in that order, so the surrender lands at the moment nothing is left to hold instead. Then the sentence narrows to a smaller group: those who did not merely refuse but obstructed others from the path. Their punishment is described as stacked on top, and the reason given is the damage done rather than the belief held.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just shown the partners disowning those who called upon them, and this completes the scene. The classical commentators connect the second ayah to the organised effort in Mecca to keep others away from the message, including pressure on individuals and on pilgrims arriving for the season. They describe the practice generally rather than tying the ayah to one episode.

keyTerms.note: A noun from the root for peace and for handing something over. It names the act with no word for regret attached, which is why commentators distinguish it from turning back in repentance.

keyTerms.gloss: went astray, was lost to them
keyTerms.note: The verb ordinarily used of a person losing their way. Applied here to the inventions, it reverses the usual direction: what was followed is now the thing that has gone missing.
A verb for spoiling something that was sound. It names outward damage rather than inward refusal, which is why the added punishment attaches to it and not to disbelief on its own.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Access to the sanctuary at Mecca was controlled, and the men who controlled it also controlled who could speak to the pilgrims arriving each season. Warnings were given at the approaches, and anyone showing interest could be pressured through family and through trade. Obstruction was not abstract. It was a practical business run by people whose income depended on the arrangement.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase used here for the additional penalty, punishment above punishment, occurs only once in the Quran. Elsewhere the language of increase is more general. Classical commentators noted that this stacking matches the double charge stated in the same ayah, refusal and obstruction, with one placed literally on top of the other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage draws a line between surrender that is chosen and surrender that is left over, and it places the value of faith firmly on the near side of that line. It then separates two kinds of wrongdoing. Refusing for yourself is one thing; standing between other people and a road is treated as a further act with its own consequence, which makes obstruction a category rather than an intensity.

crossReferences.why: Describes belief professed once the punishment is seen, and says it did not benefit them then.
Sets up this scene, with the partners disowning those who used to call upon them.
Names those who disbelieved and turned others from the path, exactly as this ayah does.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time you gave in only when there was nothing left to hold, and notice how different that felt from choosing. Then pick one small thing you have been holding out on and let it go now, while it still costs you something. That difference is the entire subject of this passage.

studies.title: An Explanation Of All Things
studies.meaning: The witness scene returns, now with the addressee himself named as a witness over the people in front of him. Then the sentence turns to the book and gives it four descriptions in a row: an explanation of everything, guidance, mercy, and good news. The commentators differ over how widely to read the first, most limiting it to what concerns religion rather than to every subject. The list ends on good news rather than on warning.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This ayah repeats an earlier one in the surah with additions, which the classical commentators note as deliberate rather than accidental. The scene of witnesses answers an audience that expected intercession from figures it had honoured. No specific occasion is reported for the ayah, and it works as the summary immediately before the surah's most quoted instruction.

keyTerms.note: A legal word for someone who testifies to what they saw. Used twice in this ayah, it frames the day as a hearing at which testimony comes from inside each community rather than from outside.
An intensive noun from the verb to make plain, which this surah has already used twice of the messenger's own task. Here the quality is transferred from the person to the book itself.
From the same root as the birth announcement earlier in this surah. Placing it last means the description of the book ends on the note that the earlier passage showed a man refusing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony was everything in a society without archives. Contracts, marriages, debts and blood settlements lived in the memory of named witnesses, and a man's value as a witness was a real form of standing. Choosing a witness from within a community rather than a stranger matched the practice exactly, since an outsider's account of a clan's affairs carried very little weight.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah repeats the opening of one five ayat earlier, changing a single preposition and then continuing differently. The earlier version leaves the witness unnamed and closes with excuses refused. This one names the addressee as a witness and closes with guidance, mercy and good news. The same sentence is turned twice within one page.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing the book's description immediately after the courtroom scene links the two. A text that explains is what makes testimony fair, since a community cannot be witnessed against over something never made clear to it. Naming mercy and good news alongside guidance then resists any reading of scripture as primarily a legal instrument, even in a passage whose setting is a hearing.

crossReferences.why: States the same raising of witnesses five ayat earlier, without the additions made here.
Puts the same scene as a question, each community brought a witness and the messenger over them.
Calls the Book sent down something explained in detail, close to the description used here.

studies.applyIt: Read the surah you know best in translation, from beginning to end, in one sitting this week. Not to study it. The claim in this ayah is that the book explains, and explanation needs continuity, which is exactly what reading in fragments removes. Give one surah its whole shape once and see what changes.

studies.title: Three Commanded, Three Forbidden
studies.meaning: Six things in one sentence, arranged as three and three. Justice is giving what is owed; the second term goes beyond it, meaning to do what is excellent whether or not it is due; the third narrows to relatives specifically, so kindness begins where it is hardest to sustain. Against these stand gross indecency, what is commonly recognised as wrong, and overreach against others. The sentence closes not with a threat but with the word for counsel.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, near the end of a surah that has spent its length on blessings, argument and the conduct of communities. The classical sources report no occasion for the ayah itself, though they preserve accounts of its effect on hearers, including a well-known report of a Meccan opponent moved by it. It sits immediately before instructions about keeping covenants and oaths, which gives the general statement an immediate application.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to make two things equal in weight. It is the balance point rather than generosity, which is why the next word is needed to carry the sentence past mere fairness.
From the root for beauty and goodness. It covers both doing a thing well and doing well by someone, and it names a surplus above what justice requires rather than a softening of it.
The root means to seek or desire, and in this form it names wanting past your share at someone else's cost. It is the social form of the arrogance the surah has already been describing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca had no court and no police. Disputes were settled by clan pressure, arbitration by a respected figure, and the threat of feud, which meant a strong family could take more than its share and a weak one had little recourse. Obligations to relatives were the strongest social bond there was, and also the most easily exploited. Naming justice, excellence and kinship in one line addressed exactly where that system broke.
studies.didYouKnow: A companion of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is reported to have called this the most comprehensive verse in the Quran for good and evil. In many places it is recited from the pulpit at the close of the Friday address, a custom that goes back centuries. The ayah names six things and not one of them concerns ritual.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah presents ethics as something commanded rather than deduced, and then declines to argue for it. What it establishes is that the moral content of revelation is not a separate department from belief: the same voice that has spent the surah describing rain and cattle now describes conduct, in the same register. The final word matters too. Instruction is given as counsel aimed at remembering, which assumes the hearer already knows.

crossReferences.why: Takes justice to its hardest case, standing for it against yourself and your own family.
Warns that hatred of a people must not push you off fairness towards them.
Names the same claim of the relative, set beside the poor and the traveller.

studies.applyIt: Take the third item on the list, the relative. Pick the family member you have the least warmth for and give them something this week that justice does not require: a call with no agenda, a small errand, an unprompted piece of praise. The ayah puts kinship next to justice for a reason. It is where being merely fair stops being enough.

studies.title: You Made God Your Guarantor
studies.meaning: An instruction about covenants is followed by a prohibition about oaths, and then by the sentence that gives both their weight. When you swear, you have already named God as the party standing surety for the agreement. The commentators note that this is not presented as a threat but as a description of what an oath structurally is. The closing clause about knowledge sits exactly where a human witness would otherwise be named.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, though the classical commentators observe that the surah's closing section addresses the practical conduct of a community and reads naturally beside the pledges given to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). They report no single occasion for this ayah. Oaths and treaties were the load-bearing structure of Arabian life, which is why a passage about them needs no introduction.

keyTerms.note: A verb from the language of completing a payment. It treats a covenant as a debt that can be partly discharged, so falling short is described as underpayment rather than as betrayal.
From a root for making something firm. It names the deliberate strengthening of an oath, so the prohibition covers promises the speaker took extra trouble to make binding.
The legal term for a third party who answers for a debt if the principal defaults. It occurs only here in the Quran, and it describes the oath's structure rather than adding a penalty.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Without courts or written records, an oath was the enforcement mechanism. Alliances, safe passage, debts and the ending of feuds all rested on sworn word, reinforced by a guarantor who would pay or fight if the swearer failed. Finding a guarantor was itself a negotiation, and a man who could not find one could not make agreements at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a guarantor occurs only once in the Quran, and it is here. Its ordinary use in that society was commercial: the person who accepts liability if a debtor defaults. So an oath is described using the exact legal term a Meccan trader would have used in a contract, with the roles left unchanged.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes an oath a three-party arrangement rather than a two-party one, and that changes what breaking it is. It is not only a wrong done to the other person but a claim made against a guarantor who was named without being consulted. That is why the instruction needs no penalty clause. The structure of the act supplies the seriousness, and the ayah only has to describe it accurately.

crossReferences.why: Returns to the same subject three ayat later, with the consequence of deceit spelled out.
Opens with the same instruction to fulfil covenants, at the head of a surah about agreements.
Says the covenant will be asked about, adding the accounting this ayah leaves implicit.

studies.applyIt: Find the smallest promise you have let slide, the kind nobody would ever hold you to, and keep it this week. Reply to the message. Return the thing. This ayah puts the weight on the structure of a promise rather than on its size, which means the small ones are not a different category, only a quieter one.

studies.title: She Unravelled Her Own Yarn
studies.meaning: A comparison arrives without introduction: a woman who spins thread up to strength and then pulls it back into loose fibre. What makes it sting is that nobody did this to her. Then the application, which is oaths used as a way in, and a motive named plainly, one group being wealthier than another. The commentators note that the closing clause reframes the entire situation as a test rather than as a temptation.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan by placement, though the classical commentators note the ayah's concern with agreements between groups. Some report a proverbial figure in Mecca who spun and then unspun her thread; others read the comparison as constructed rather than drawn from a known person. The sources preserve both readings without settling between them, and no single occasion is agreed.

keyTerms.note: The same verb used in the ayah just before for breaking oaths. Applying it first to thread and then to promises makes the comparison structural rather than decorative, since one word does both jobs.
The word occurs only here in the Quran. It names spun thread taken back to the state it held before spinning, so what has been lost is the work rather than the material itself.
From a root for entering. It names something slipped into an agreement to leave the swearer a way in, and it occurs only in this surah, twice within three ayat.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Spinning was continuous women's work, done while walking, talking and watching children, and a household's cloth depended on it. Thread was spun on a drop spindle over days and then woven or traded. Undoing spun yarn needed no explanation to anyone: it was the most visible possible waste of accumulated labour, and everyone had handled a spindle's worth of it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the undone fibres occurs only here in the Quran, and the verb describing what she does to them is the same one used in the previous ayah for breaking an oath. The comparison is built by repeating a single verb across two objects, thread and promise, without any statement that the two are alike.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming the motive as one community being wealthier than another is unusually specific. It identifies the pressure that actually breaks agreements, which is advantage rather than malice, and it does so without moralising about it. Calling the whole arrangement a test then places the inequality itself inside the design. What is being examined is not whether you were offered a better deal but what you did when you were.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb for breaking oaths that this ayah applies to unravelling spun thread.
Describes a people who broke their oaths after agreement, and asks whether they will be feared.
Sets those who keep the covenant against those who cut apart what should be joined.

studies.applyIt: Think of one relationship you have quietly downgraded because a better option appeared. A friend, a supplier, a commitment. You do not have to undo the newer arrangement. Just tell the older party the truth about where things stand, this week, rather than letting it fray. Unravelling is slower than cutting and looks less like a decision.

studies.title: One Community If He Willed
studies.meaning: A conditional that is deliberately not carried out. God could have made everyone a single community, and did not. What follows is stated in the most compressed possible form, leaving astray and guiding, both attached to His will. The commentators are careful here, reading the leaving astray in the light of a turning away that precedes it. The last clause then restores accountability, which is what stops the ayah collapsing into fatalism.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, inside the section on oaths and communities, where the surah has just named one group's prosperity as the pressure that breaks agreements. The classical commentators read the ayah as addressing the plurality surrounding those agreements, and they report no particular occasion. The surah raised a similar conditional earlier, but placed in the mouths of objectors rather than stated directly.

keyTerms.note: A group defined by something shared rather than by descent. Its use lets the sentence be about religious division rather than tribal division, which the audience heard as two separate matters.
A causative that the commentators consistently qualify. They read it alongside ayat describing the turning away that comes first, so the leaving follows a movement the person has already made.
An emphatic passive carrying two separate markers of certainty. Its position at the very end holds the ayah in balance, since a questioning implies an answer belonging to the one questioned.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia held many communities at once: tribes with their own gods, Jewish settlements in the north, Christian towns to the south, and individuals who had rejected all of it. Trade required dealing across every one of those lines. Nobody in that audience imagined a single religious community as the natural state of things, which is what makes this conditional so pointed.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah raises the same conditional twice, and the two occurrences sit in different mouths. Earlier it is quoted from objectors arguing that had God willed, they would not have served anything besides Him. Here it is stated directly, and what follows is a questioning rather than an excuse.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah places divine will and human accountability in one sentence and declines to reconcile them. That refusal is the position rather than an evasion of it. What it rules out is using either half against the other: you cannot appeal to the will as an excuse, because the questioning is stated outright, and you cannot claim your guidance as an achievement, because the guiding is attributed. Both moves close at once.

crossReferences.why: Quotes objectors making the same conditional, and answers that the messengers' duty was delivery.
States the same possibility and adds that people will not cease to differ from one another.
Asks whether the messenger would compel people, once the same point has been made.

studies.applyIt: The next time you are certain about why someone else has not been guided, stop at the certainty. This ayah attributes both directions to God's will and then says you will be asked about your own conduct, not theirs. Spend the energy you were about to spend diagnosing them on one thing you have been putting off yourself.

studies.title: A Foot That Slips
studies.meaning: The prohibition returns with its consequences laid out. Oaths used as a way in cause a foot to slip after it had been steady, and the harm is described as tasted, which makes it personal before it is punitive. Then the reason widens to hindering others from the path. The second ayah names the transaction underneath the whole business, exchanging a covenant for a small price, and no price is said to be large enough.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah's closing instructions address a community that had to trade and travel among people who did not share its commitments, where a broken oath was both a practical betrayal and a public argument against the message. The classical commentators report no specific occasion, and read the pair as continuing an instruction given a few ayat earlier in the same section.

keyTerms.note: The verb for a foot losing purchase on smooth ground. It makes the failure look sudden and involuntary, although the ayah has just described the deliberate act that brought it about.
A noun for standing fixed. Naming the security before the slip means what is lost was already held, which is a different injury from never having had it in the first place.
The commercial word for what is paid in an exchange. Calling it small names no amount; it says that whatever the figure was, the thing given up was not of that order.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A merchant's reputation for keeping his word was his working capital. It determined whether he could take goods on credit in the north, whether a tribe would guarantee his passage, and whether anyone would partner with him next season. Selling that reputation for one profitable deception was a recognised temptation and a recognised stupidity, discussed in the market like any other bad trade.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase describing oaths used as a means of deception occurs twice in the Quran, and both occurrences are in this surah, three ayat apart. The instruction is given, then the comparison about unravelled thread is placed between them, and then the identical phrase returns with its consequences attached.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Framing the matter as a purchase is the passage's real move. It concedes that breaking a covenant is done for something, that the something is real, and that it can be weighed. What it denies is that the weighing was ever done honestly, because what is with God was left out of the calculation. The argument is therefore about arithmetic rather than about resisting a temptation.

crossReferences.why: Gives the instruction this passage restates, naming the guarantor rather than the consequence.
Describes those who exchange the covenant of God and their own oaths for a small price.
Uses the same phrase about not selling what has been revealed for a small price.

studies.applyIt: Look at one thing you have gained recently by shading the truth, even slightly. Price it honestly: what you got, and what you spent to get it. This passage does not ask you to be above the trade. It asks you to do the sum properly, which most people avoid because the answer turns out to be obvious.

studies.title: What Runs Out And What Stays
studies.meaning: A comparison stated as plainly as Arabic allows, with no image and no argument. What is in your possession is described by a verb of exhaustion, the emptying of a well or a purse. What is with God is described by a participle of remaining. Then a promise is attached, and its terms are unexpected: the patient are repaid according to the best of what they did, not the average and not the worst.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayah closes a passage about oaths and covenants, where the temptation named is exchanging an agreement with God for a small price. The commentators read this as addressing people under pressure to renounce their faith for money, protection or standing, which was a live situation in Mecca. No particular occasion is reported. The preceding ayah has already said that what is with God is better, and this one says why.

keyTerms.note: A verb used of supplies that finish and of a well that gives no more. It says nothing about how much there was, only that the quantity is of a kind that ends.
An active participle from the root behind one of the divine names, the Everlasting. Using it of what is with God ties the durability of the reward to the durability of the one holding it.
A superlative, not a general word for good. The reckoning is described as taking the highest point of a person's record as the rate for the whole of it, which is a specific and unusual arrangement.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in that economy was perishable in obvious ways. Grain went to weevils, dates fermented, camels died of thirst or were driven off in a raid, and a merchant's whole capital could be one caravan crossing hostile country. Nobody had to be persuaded that possessions run out; they watched it happen. What the ayah adds is a second column in the same ledger, held somewhere the raiders cannot reach.
studies.didYouKnow: The closing clause of this ayah is repeated almost word for word at the end of the next one, which promises a good life to whoever acts rightly. Repeating an ending across two consecutive ayat binds them into a pair, so the reward for patience and the reward for righteous work are given identical terms. The device appears elsewhere in the Quran but rarely this tightly.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets up a comparison between two holdings and then, instead of naming what the lasting one contains, names who receives it. That is a deliberate withholding: the reward is defined by its permanence and by its rate, not by its content. And the rate is mercy expressed as arithmetic. Being repaid at the level of your best moments rather than your typical ones says something about how the accounting is intended to come out.

crossReferences.why: States the same contrast, adding that what is with God is better and more lasting.
Everything on earth passes away, and only the face of your Lord remains.
Calls wealth and children the ornament of this life and lasting deeds the better hope.

studies.applyIt: Look at your bank balance and then at your calendar for this week. One of those runs out and one of them is where the other column gets filled. Find twenty minutes in the calendar you were going to spend on nothing much, and give it to something that will still matter in ten years. A person, usually, rather than a project.

studies.title: The Promise Of A Good Life
studies.meaning: The condition is stated three ways and each one is doing work. Righteous action is required, male or female is specified so that no one is admitted by category, and belief is named as the accompanying state rather than as a separate act. What is promised is a good life, and the commentators differ on where it is located: some read it of this world, as contentment, sufficiency and lawful provision; others of the grave or the hereafter. Most allow both.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the closing movement of the surah, among instructions about oaths, covenants and how to bear pressure. The audience included women who had accepted the message against their households and men who had lost trade and protection for it. Stating the promise for male and female in the same clause was not abstract in that setting. The classical sources report no specific occasion for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: The adjective means wholesome, clean and pleasant, the same word used of good soil and good speech. It describes the quality of a life rather than its length or its comfort, which is why the commentators could locate it in either world.

The verb is to give life, not to grant or provide. Coupled with an oath particle and an emphatic ending, it reads as a guarantee, and it implies the good life is something conferred rather than achieved.

From a root meaning to be fit, whole and in good repair, used of a mended tool or a reconciled quarrel. Righteous action in Arabic is action that repairs something, which is a more concrete idea than being good.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A woman's standing in that society came through her father, her husband and her sons, and her religious life was largely her household's. A slave's was his owner's. So a sentence that assigns the same promise to male and female on the same terms cut across the ordinary way merit was assigned. Some of the earliest believers were women and slaves, and the sentence would have been heard by them first.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of male and female in a promise of reward occurs several times in the Quran, and in each case the wording is symmetrical rather than additive: the same condition, the same recompense, no separate clause. Here the ayah also switches from singular to plural halfway through, moving from him to them, which widens the promise from the individual to the group.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are being fixed. The first is that the standing of a human being before God does not run through sex, lineage or social position, since the qualifying terms are action and belief and nothing else. The second is quieter: the reward begins with a life rather than a place. Whatever the good life is, it is described as something God gives now, in the same sentence as the reward that comes later.

crossReferences.why: Lists ten qualities twice over, once for men and once for women, in the same terms.
Whoever does good, male or female, and is a believer, enters the garden.
Names the opposite condition, a life made narrow by turning from the reminder.

studies.applyIt: Pick one action today that repairs rather than adds. Fix the drawer that sticks, answer the message you have been avoiding, apologise for a small thing nobody else remembers. The word this ayah uses for righteous action is built on the idea of putting something back in working order, and it is easier to start there than with anything grander.

studies.title: Seek Refuge Before You Read
studies.meaning: An instruction about how to approach recitation, followed by two ayat explaining why it is needed and why it works. The seeking of refuge comes before the reading rather than during it. Then the reach of what is being guarded against is described twice, once by denial and once by limitation, and both descriptions turn on relationship rather than on strength. The commentators note that no power to compel is attributed anywhere in the three ayat.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, placed just after the surah's instructions on oaths and just before its answer to the charge of forgery. The classical commentators read that position as deliberate, since the ayat which follow concern people misreading the revelation. They report no particular occasion. The practice of saying these words before recitation is drawn from this ayah and is attested very early.

keyTerms.note: A verb for going to someone stronger and placing yourself under their cover. In that society it named a formal act with obligations attached, so the word describes entering a protection rather than making a request.
A passive form from a root for stoning and casting away. It describes a status already imposed rather than a threat still open, so the adversary is named by his expulsion.
A word for delegated power backed by proof. Denying it says the influence described has no standing rather than no force, which is why the next ayah defines it by who accepts it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Seeking refuge was a legal act with a name. A man in danger could go to a stronger clan and formally place himself under its protection, and once accepted, an attack on him became an attack on his protectors. Refusing such a request damaged a chief's reputation. Everyone who heard this instruction knew exactly what entering a protection involved.
studies.didYouKnow: The name used for the adversary here, the driven-out one, occurs only twice in the Quran. The other occurrence sits inside the prayer of a woman placing her newborn daughter and that child's descendants under God's protection, so both uses of the phrase fall within an act of seeking refuge.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The three ayat together describe an adversary with no jurisdiction. Authority is denied over those who believe and trust, and then granted only over those who take him as an ally, which makes the relationship voluntary on the human side. That places responsibility somewhere uncomfortable and reassuring at once. Nothing is imposed, so nothing can be blamed, and the protection asked for is already available.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction for the moment a prompting arrives, using the identical verb.
Holds the only other use of this name for the adversary, inside a mother's prayer of protection.
Has him admit at the end that he held no authority over anyone, only an invitation.

studies.applyIt: Say the words of refuge aloud the next time you open the Quran, and then pause for one breath before you begin reading. The pause is the point. The instruction places the asking before the reading rather than inside it, which makes it a way of arriving rather than something done while already moving.

studies.title: A Sign In Place Of A Sign
studies.meaning: A practice is described and an accusation quoted in the same sentence. When one revealed passage is put in the place of another, the objection raised is not confusion but forgery, and the commentators read the charge as being about consistency: a man inventing would keep his story straight. The parenthesis in the middle answers it before the accusation is even reported, and the closing clause identifies the real shortfall as knowledge.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical commentators differ over the exact scope of what is being substituted, some reading it of rulings and others more broadly of passages, and that discussion is long and never settled. What is agreed is the objection reported here, raised in Mecca against the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) as evidence that the revelation was his own composition.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for putting one thing in place of another. The grammar makes God the agent, which is the whole answer to the charge, since a substitution with a known author is not a slip.
The same word covers a revealed passage and a sign in creation. Its double sense keeps this sentence connected to the signs the surah has been listing for dozens of ayat before it.
An active participle from a root for cutting something to shape. The accusation is of manufacture rather than of error, so what is alleged is deliberate work and not a mistake.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poetry was the culture's memory, and audiences policed it closely. A reciter who altered a line between performances was corrected from the floor, and inconsistency was the standard way of exposing someone reciting from invention rather than from transmission. The objection quoted here used a test the audience trusted, applied to a text arriving across years rather than delivered whole.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for what is substituted is the same one the surah has been using for the signs in creation: rain, cattle, birds and the turning of shadows. The objection and the argument share a single vocabulary, so a passage replaced and a bird held up in the air are named by one term.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The parenthesis carries the weight, and it is not a defence of any particular substitution. It states that the one revealing knows what He sends down, which moves the question from the content to the sender. That is a claim about revelation as an act rather than as a text, and it makes disclosure over time a feature of teaching rather than evidence of a changing mind.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle directly, that nothing is replaced except with something like it or better.
Says God erases and confirms what He wills, and that the source of the book is with Him.
Reminds the messenger that what was given could be taken away entirely, had God willed it.

studies.applyIt: Think of an instruction you were given as a child that was later replaced with a better one, by a parent or a teacher who knew more than you did at the time. Notice that you did not conclude they had been lying. Hold that experience beside this ayah once, and see whether the objection still feels as strong.

studies.title: Brought Down In Truth
studies.meaning: A reply is dictated rather than argued. The answer to the charge of invention is a claim about transmission: the revelation was brought down by a named bearer, from the hearer's own Lord, and truthfully. Then three purposes follow, and the first of them is unexpected. It is to make firm those who already believe, which means the reply is addressed as much to a community under pressure as to the objectors outside it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, answering the accusation reported in the ayah just before. The classical commentators identify the bearer named here with the angel Gabriel, and note that the same title is used elsewhere in the Quran in connection with Jesus. The setting is the late Meccan period, when the small community was under sustained pressure and the charge of forgery was being made publicly.

keyTerms.note: A title the classical commentators identify with the angel Gabriel. It occurs four times in the Quran, and this is the only occurrence that concerns the descent of the revelation itself.

keyTerms.gloss: so that He may make firm
keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for planting something so it will not shift. It names an effect on people who already believe, which is why the ayah reads as support rather than as proof.
A phrase covering both accuracy and rightful entitlement. Attached to the bringing down, it says the transmission was faithful and also that it was authorised, answering two objections at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A message's authority in that world depended on its chain. A tribal messenger was asked who sent him and by whose hand the words had travelled, and a claim without a named carrier was worth nothing. Answering an accusation of invention by naming the bearer was exactly the form of response the audience expected, even where they refused the particular answer given.
studies.didYouKnow: The title used here for the bearer occurs four times in the Quran. The other three all concern Jesus, who is described as strengthened by this same Spirit. This is the only place where the title is attached to the sending down of the revelation to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming a bearer places revelation inside a chain of transmission rather than inside a private experience, and that has consequences. What is claimed can be described, disputed and tested against itself, which is what the surrounding ayat immediately proceed to do. Listing the strengthening of believers first also concedes something honest: the immediate work of revelation is often to hold the people who already accepted it.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same title of the one who strengthened Jesus, in a passage about messengers rejected.
Describes the same descent, naming the trustworthy spirit and a clear Arabic tongue.
Reports the accusation of invention that this ayah is dictated in order to answer.

studies.applyIt: When something you believe is challenged, notice whether your first move is to defend the content or to check where you got it. This ayah answers a charge by naming a source rather than by arguing the point. Try that order once this week on something small, and see how much of the argument it quietly removes.

studies.title: A Clear Arabic Tongue
studies.meaning: A rumour is quoted and answered with a single observation about language. Someone had suggested a human teacher, and the reply does not deny that the person existed or that conversations took place. It points instead at the distance between that man's speech and the text in question. The commentators report several identifications for the person alluded to and preserve the range, since the argument does not depend on which is correct.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical sources name several possibilities for the person referred to, generally a non-Arab living in Mecca, and they differ over which is meant. What they agree on is the shape of the accusation, which conceded the quality of what was being recited and went looking for a human origin for it. No single identification is settled in the sources.

keyTerms.note: A verb for deviating from a straight line, used of leaning towards something. The word carries a sense of bending away from the obvious, so the allusion is described as a swerve rather than a claim.
A word describing speech that is hard to follow rather than merely a foreigner. It names the man by how he sounded, which is precisely the ground on which the reply stands.
An active participle, so the tongue does not merely happen to be clear but makes things clear. It is the same form the surah has used of the messenger's task and of the book's function.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was full of foreigners: enslaved people from Abyssinia and Persia, traders from Syria, craftsmen who had settled and married. Several spoke Arabic imperfectly and worked at trades near the sanctuary. A rumour that one of them was the real source travelled easily, because a foreign teacher was a more comfortable explanation for people who had already conceded the recitation's quality.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for the non-Arab tongue appears three times in the Quran, and one of those occurrences imagines the opposite case, asking what people would have said had the revelation come in a foreign tongue to Arab hearers. The same word carries the accusation in one place and the answer to it in another.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply argues from craft rather than from authority, which is unusual and deliberate. It invites the objector to compare two samples of language and draw the obvious conclusion, and it accepts in advance that the comparison is one anybody can make. That places part of the case for revelation in something publicly available, which matters for a claim that could otherwise rest entirely on the claimant.

crossReferences.why: Imagines the reverse case, a foreign recitation to Arab hearers, and the objection that would follow.
Says that had a non-Arab recited it to them, they would not have believed in it.
Reports a related charge, that others helped him and that these were old legends written down.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you reach for an explanation because it is more comfortable rather than because it fits. The rumour answered here was not stupid; it was convenient. Ask yourself once this week, about something you believe lightly, whether you took it up because it was true or because the alternative was harder.

studies.title: Who Actually Invents Lies
studies.meaning: The accusation of forgery is turned around without heat. Two parallel sentences do the work: those who do not believe in the signs are not guided, and it is those same people who fabricate. The commentators note that the argument turns on motive and habit rather than on logic. Someone with nothing at stake beyond this world has a reason to invent; someone staking everything on an account of the next has the strongest possible reason not to.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, immediately after the charge that a human teacher stood behind the recitation. The surah has spent several ayat answering that accusation, and here it returns it. The classical commentators read the pair as closing the exchange rather than opening a new subject, and report no specific occasion. The surrounding ayat all concern the same public dispute in Mecca.

keyTerms.note: The same verb used against the messenger a few ayat earlier. Repeating it with a different subject is the whole argument, since the charge is returned in the vocabulary in which it arrived.
Definite rather than indefinite, so the sentence names lying as a category rather than a particular untruth. What is being described is a practice, not an isolated incident.
A definite plural in the emphatic final position. Arabic uses this construction for restriction, so the sentence does not merely say that they lie but that they are the ones who do.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a society without documents, character was the evidence. Disputes were settled by weighing the standing of the parties, and a man known for accuracy could win against one known for embellishment without either producing anything. Returning an accusation by pointing at who had a record of inventing was a recognised move, and the audience knew how to weigh it.
studies.didYouKnow: The root for fabricating runs through this surah in both directions. It is used first of what people invent about God, then in the objectors' accusation against the messenger, and then twice of the objectors themselves. One word carries the charge out and brings it back within a few pages.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes truthfulness a matter of what a person has staked rather than of temperament. It does not claim that believers cannot lie. It claims that someone who does not believe the signs has removed the only consideration that would make inventing about God costly. That reframes the dispute entirely: the question is not who sounds more sincere but who has anything to lose.

crossReferences.why: Holds the accusation of invention that these two ayat answer by returning it to the accusers.
Asks who does greater wrong than one who invents a lie about God after truth has reached him.
Puts the same question, pairing invention about God with denial of His signs.

studies.applyIt: Ask what a claim would cost the person making it. Not whether they seem honest, which is easy to perform, but what they lose if it turns out to be false. Apply that test to one thing you were told this week and one thing you said. It is the test this passage uses, and it works in both directions.

studies.title: A Heart At Rest In Faith
studies.meaning: A general statement opens and is interrupted before it can close, and the interruption is the point. An exception is inserted for the person compelled whose heart remains settled, and only then does the sentence resume and describe the other case, someone who opened his chest to it willingly. The commentators read the contrast as lying between what a mouth says under force and what a person has actually made room for inside.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the period of persecution before the emigration. The classical sources report an occasion in which a member of the early community, tortured until he spoke words of denial, came afterwards in distress and was reassured. The sources describe that episode consistently in outline. The ayah is read as establishing a general principle rather than a single dispensation for one person.

keyTerms.note: A passive from the root for aversion, so the word already contains the person's unwillingness. The grammar removes agency, which is exactly the ground on which the exception is standing.

A word for something that has come to stillness after motion, used of a heart and of a town at peace. It describes a condition rather than an assertion, so it is not something a person can simply claim.
A verb for cutting something open and making it broader. Used of the chest it describes making interior room, which is why commentators treat it as the opposite of speech extracted under pressure.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The early community in Mecca included people with no clan behind them, and they bore the worst of it, since violence against a protected man brought retaliation and violence against an unprotected one brought none at all. Those without patrons could be held and beaten with no recourse anywhere. The distinction this ayah draws mattered most to precisely those people.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for the heart at rest comes from the same root as a word applied a few ayat later to a town that was secure and settled before it turned ungrateful. The same idea of stillness describes an inner state under torture and a city living in comfort, and in the surah it is the city that fails.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The exception establishes that faith is located in the heart rather than in the mouth, and the second half prevents that from becoming a licence. What is condemned is not weakness under force but having made room. The distinction lies between a person overwhelmed from outside and a person who has undergone an inward change, and the passage insists these are different things even when the words spoken are identical.

crossReferences.why: Uses a word from the same root for settled security, there of a town rather than a heart.
Allows for outward caution in a situation of danger, while locating the reality elsewhere.
Describes a man of faith concealing it among people who would have harmed him for showing it.

studies.applyIt: Think of a place where what you say and what you hold have come apart, not under threat but out of ordinary social ease. The severity of this ayah falls on the widening rather than on the words. Notice whether you have started to make room for something you would once only have said, and name it accurately to yourself.

studies.title: They Preferred This Life
studies.meaning: A reason is given for what the previous ayah described, and it is not stated as unbelief but as preference. They loved this life more than the next, which makes the failure a matter of ranking rather than of information. Then a seal is described over three faculties, and the passage closes on a verdict introduced by a phrase this surah has used twice before. The commentators read the sealing as a consequence of the preference and not its cause.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following the passage that distinguished compulsion from willing change. These ayat take up the second case and explain it. The classical commentators note that the explanation offered is about attachment rather than about doctrine, which they read as characteristic of the surah's whole approach. No specific occasion is reported for any of the three ayat.

keyTerms.note: A verb for choosing between two things a person loves. The form makes it comparative, so the sentence does not accuse them of hating the next life, only of ranking this one above it.
The verb for pressing a seal into clay or wax to close something. It describes a closure that follows a decision to close, which is why commentators tie it to the preference named just before.
From a root for letting something slip out of attention. It names an absence rather than an act, so the passage ends by describing people who are not noticing rather than people who are fighting.
